bio.en: Howie Liu is the co-founder and CEO of Airtable, the flexible low-code application platform, and is part of a wave of founders reinventing decade-old software businesses for the AI era.
bio.zh: Howie Liu 是 Airtable 的联合创始人兼 CEO；Airtable 是一款灵活的低代码应用平台，他也是将成立十余年的软件公司重新改造以迎接 AI 时代的创始人之一。

summary.en: Howie exemplifies the 'IC CEO' trend—founders diving back into building themselves—and shares the specific skills he believes PMs, engineers, and designers need now (e.g., PMs becoming hybrid prototypers with design sensibility). He explains how he restructured Airtable into a 'fast-thinking' and a 'slow-thinking' group to accelerate AI investment, and how he encourages his team to cancel meetings and just experiment with AI tools. The episode is a practical playbook for navigating the existential AI transition every company is facing.
summary.zh: Howie 是“IC CEO”（创始人重新下场做具体工作）趋势的代表——他分享了认为 PM、工程师和设计师当下需要的具体技能（例如 PM 要变成兼具设计感的混合原型师）。他解释了如何把 Airtable 重组成“快思考”和“慢思考”两个组以加速 AI 投入，以及他如何鼓励团队取消会议、去亲手试用 AI 工具。这期节目是应对每家公司都在经历的 AI 生存转型的实用手册。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu

turns.zh: 如果你想取消一天或一周的所有会议，专心试用所有你认为可能与Airtable相关的AI产品，那就去试试吧。

turns.zh: 这其实更多取决于个人的态度。上述三个角色中，能跨界融合其他两个角色的人会占据明显优势。作为产品经理，你需要逐渐转变为既能原型设计又有优秀设计审美的混合型PM。

turns.en: Yeah, right about 13.

turns.en: 13 years. I imagine there've been a lot of ups and a lot of downs. I want to talk about all those things. I want to talk about a lot of the lessons that you've learned along the way. I want to start with what I imagine was a very surprising down moment in the history of Airtable. This is something that, unfortunately, something I think about when I think of Airtable. I feel other people may feel this way, is there's this tweet that went super viral, maybe a couple of years ago at this point where someone just shared all this data and they're like, Airtable is dead. (00:04:57): They've raised way more money than they're worth. They're not making enough to get from underwater. Yeah, Airtable RIP. What happened there? How much of that was true? How did that go?
turns.zh: 13年。我能想象其中既有高光时刻，也有低谷。我想聊聊这些经历，聊聊你一路走来获得的经验教训。首先我想谈谈Airtable历史上一个令人震惊的低谷时刻。说起来挺遗憾的，每当我想到Airtable时，总会想起那条疯传的推文。大概两年前，有人分享了一堆数据，然后写道“Airtable死了”。（00:04:57）他们声称Airtable融资远超其估值，增长速度不足以摆脱困境。最后还说Airtable安息吧。这是怎么回事？这些说法有多少是真实的？后来情况如何？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, so basically none of it was true. I mean, the surprising thing to me was how viral this tweet went when ... Frankly, I actually look back at this person's other tweets. I think they worked at CB Insights, and the irony is the whole point of that business is to have good data, good data quality around private company data. And they just literally had incorrect numbers by a strong multiple on what our revenue scale was, what our growth rate was. And if it gave me some consolation, I look back and this person had also tweeted about other companies, like Flexport was the last take-down tweet. (00:05:45): They have like, "Oh, Flexport's dead" and their evaluation is too high, and blah, blah, blah. And so, I think that the more surprising thing was just like this person has been tweeting a bunch of spicy takes that are not substantiated by real data or correct data, and yet this particular tweet went super viral and that was the perplexing part to me. And then, actually, I think what really gave it legs was on the All In podcast, which is obviously super popular. And I listened to it. They covered it. They were like, "Oh, latest on this week's news, this tweet about Airtable. What do we think about this?" (00:06:22): And it almost, I think became a way to talk about a broader theme of what happens to this last generation of highly valued companies, maybe decacorn companies in this new ... And at that point, it was the recent moment for both public and private markets. They did also issue a correction though. All In, did a follow-up episode, a few, I think weeks later saying, "Hey, we got the numbers wrong. We are revising our case and a view on Airtable."
turns.zh: 基本上一句都不属实。最让我惊讶的是那条推文传播得如此之广……说实话，我回看那人的其他推文。他曾在CB Insights工作，讽刺的是这家公司的核心业务就是提供优质的私营公司数据。结果他却把我们的营收规模和增长率严重错误化了。好在能让我稍感欣慰的是，我发现他之前也攻击过其他公司，比如Flexport的推文。（00:05:45）他们声称Flexport估值过高之类的。最令人费解的是，那个人发了一堆未经核实的言论，偏偏这条推文疯传了。后来在《All In》播客上，这事儿被大肆讨论。他们甚至把这当作一个话题，探讨新兴独角兽公司（包括Airtable）的命运。当时正值公私市场低迷期。不过Airtable后来确实发了声明纠正错误，《All In》几周后又追踪报道，表示“数据有误，调整对Airtable评价”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's that line about how a lie gets around the world some number of times before truth has even this time to get out of bed?
turns.zh: 那句话怎么说来着？谎言总比真相传播得更快。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I think I learned about memes and morality very quickly in that experience. Not a very good social media person, but I think I learned a little more.
turns.zh: 是啊。这次经历让我很快领悟到社交媒体与道德的矛盾。我算不上善于玩转社交媒体，但确实学到了不少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's tough. Twitter is such ... The incentives are so misaligned. It's just I tweet something people want to share, not truth.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很艰难。推特的激励机制太不合理了。我发的东西人们爱转发，但不一定是真相。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Well, especially ... I mean, there's a lot to like ... I would say, I like the post Elon Twitter more than the pre Elon Twitter because it is just bolder, and I guess I really admire bold product execution where you're not just stuck to the current laurels and they've made so many changes, but I do feel like I get injected into my feed very sensational content all the time, and I mean, it works on me. I can't help but to click on it and engage with it, but it does ... I think it does result in this kind of content, really spreading.
turns.zh: 嗯，特别是……我是说，有很多值得喜欢的地方……我得说，比起埃隆之前的推特，我更喜欢他执掌后的推特，因为它更大胆。我想我真的很钦佩这种大胆的产品执行力——不拘泥于现有成就，不断做出改变。不过我确实觉得自己的推送里总被推送一些很吸引眼球的内容，坦白说，这对我很有效。我忍不住要点击互动，但这确实……我觉得这类内容确实传播得很快。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: For sure.

I want to go in a completely different direction, something that I'm really excited to talk to you about, which is this very emerging trend that I've noticed that I feel like you're at the forefront of CEOs becoming ICs again. It's kind of this move of, IC CEOs. CEOs getting their hands dirty again, building again, getting in the weeds, coating again. I feel like you're again at the forefront of this. Talk about just why you've done this, why you think this is important, and just what that looks like day to day to you versus what your life was like a few years ago.
turns.zh: 好的，我想换个完全不同的话题，我特别兴奋能跟你聊聊我注意到的一个新兴趋势——CEO们正重新回归成为IC（全栈开发者）。这种趋势就是，IC CEO们重新亲力亲为，参与开发，深入技术细节，重新动手编码。我觉得你在这方面走在前沿。能谈谈你为什么这么做吗？你为什么觉得这很重要？跟几年前相比，你日常的工作状态有何不同？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: The underlying reason for this shift, at least for me, is that, as we started the company, I was very much in this mode. I was literally writing code both on the backend, thinking about the real time data architecture of our platform, also the front end, the UX. And I would argue that in that founding moment, the initial product market fit finding, and especially for a product that is pure software, we weren't building an operationally heavy business like a dog walking marketplace where the tech is only an afterthought. (00:09:11): The tech was the product, right? And in a very Meta sense, Airtable is the platform for other people to build their own apps. So it's all about the attack, like the very intimate design decisions, again, both architecturally and on the front end and the product UX choices. That is the product's value prop. You can't separate those two. You can't say, "Okay, I researched the jobs to be done. Here's the workflow, here's the process, and then, okay, some engineer can just build it as an afterthought." (00:09:40): It's those little decisions and really be able to be at the bleeding edge of what's possible both in the browser and with the real-time data architecture. That made the product what it was. I think the same is true for Figma, which actually had a very parallel timeline to us. We both were founded around the same time, both spent two and a half years building the product, hands-on that early team before launching. And when I think now to both the era in between that founding moment and then now as well as now the new gen AI moment, I think there was a maturing era of both SaaS overall and Airtable specifically. (00:10:19): Where, as you scale up and you learn how to build teams and organizations and you have to scale up stuff that's not actually those intimate details, but process and people and so on, you kind of get by default further and further away from those details, right? And maybe for some businesses that's fine because no longer is it about finding the details that make for a magical new product market fit. And it is really just about scaling up an existing thing that works and using what I would call more blunt instruments to scale it up, like a more blunt roadmap, a more blunt go-to market execution strategy. (00:10:56): Regardless, I think that now, we're entering this moment where ... Certainly every software product in my opinion, has to be refounded because AI is such a paradigm shift, it's not even just like the shift from desktop to mobile or on-prem to cloud where that was more like a very one time and somewhat predictable change in form factor. I think AI is so rapidly evolving that with every evolution, every new model release and every new type of capability that's released, it actually implies novel form factors and novel UX patterns to be invented to fully capitalize on those capabilities. (00:11:36): And so to be continuously relevant and to refine product market fit in this era, I think you have to be of the details. There is no looking at it from 10,000 foot view and saying, "Oh, we're just going to throw a bunch of people at this problem." It's actually understanding what is the right product experience and the right business model that backs it up and the right ... everything else to support that engine to take advantage of the capabilities in our product domain.
turns.zh: 这种转变背后的根本原因，至少对我而言，是因为在创办公司之初，我完全处于这种状态。我当时既在后端编写代码，思考我们平台的实时数据架构，也在前端进行设计，关注用户体验。我想说，在创业初期——尤其是对于纯软件产品而言——我们并没有构建一个运营繁琐的业务，比如那种技术只是附带考虑的狗狗遛狗平台。（00:09:11）：技术本身就是产品，对吧？从更宏观的角度来看，Airtable是其他人构建自有应用的平台。因此，关键在于攻克那些技术难题——无论是架构层面的设计，还是前端和产品用户体验的选择——这才是产品的价值主张。这两者密不可分。不能说"好吧，我先研究了待办事项，制定了工作流程和流程规范，然后再让工程师来实现"。（00:09:40）：正是那些微小的决策，以及始终走在浏览器和实时数据架构技术前沿的能力，才成就了这款产品。我认为Figma也是如此。我们的创立时间非常接近，都花了两年半时间打造产品，在产品上线前打造了一个紧密协作的早期团队。如今回顾创立初期到现在，以及当前新一代AI浪潮的阶段，我认为SaaS整体和Airtable本身都经历了一个成熟期。（00:10:19）：当你扩大规模、学习如何组建团队和组织架构、不得不处理那些非核心细节（比如流程、人员管理等）时，你会自然而然地与这些细节渐行渐远。对某些企业来说，这或许无伤大雅，因为重点不再是寻找能创造神奇新产品市场的细节，而是如何将现有成功模式规模化，用更直白的路线图、更粗犷的市场策略来实现增长。（00:10:56）：无论如何，我认为我们正进入一个新的时代……在我看来，每一款软件产品都需要重新定义自身，因为AI是一场范式变革，不只是从桌面端到移动端、从本地化到云端的转变，后者更像是一次性且可预测的形态变化。AI发展迅速，每次进化、新模型发布和新能力引入，都意味着需要发明全新的交互界面和用户体验模式，才能充分发挥这些能力的价值。（00:11:36）：因此，要在当下持续保持相关性并优化产品市场匹配，我认为必须关注细节。不能以宏观视角说"我们就随便派些人去解决问题"。而是要深刻理解正确的产品体验、支持它的商业模式，以及其他所有配套要素，共同打造引擎，充分利用产品领域的能力优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this phrase somewhere where you talk about being the chief taste maker.
turns.zh: 你在某处提到自己是首席品味创造者。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to do that, you have to do exactly what you're describing.
turns.zh: 要做到这一点，你必须完全按照你所描述的去做。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: That's right. I mean, I think that, and I would also say it's actually now also hard to taste the soup without participating in at least some part of creating the soup. Meaning With AI, you can kind of look at the final product and say, "Okay, this feels right or not, or it feels like we're being bold enough and we're properly productizing these new capabilities." But I think to really understand the solution space of what's possible, you have to be in the details. (00:12:46): I mean, literally, you can't just look at screenshots or a pre-recorded video of a new product feature. AI is something you have to play with, and ideally you're playing with both the packaged up app or solution that you've built with it, but you're also playing around directly with the underlying primitives who are using the models either via API or via a chat interface. You're really pushing them to the boundaries. Because that's the only way that you really understand what these new ingredients. It's like as a chef, you just gained access to amazing new ingredients, but you have to actually get comfortable with them to put them into a new dish.
turns.zh: 没错。我的意思是，我认为现在即使不参与新功能的开发，也很难品尝到新功能带来的好处。也就是说，使用AI技术，你可以看看最终产品，然后说：“好吧，这样感觉不错，或者感觉我们做得足够大胆，成功地将这些新功能产品化了。” 但我认为，要真正理解可能的解决方案空间，你必须深入细节。（00:12:46）：我的意思是，字面上，光看截图或新产品功能的预录制视频是不够的。AI是一项需要亲身实践的技术，理想情况下，你既要使用用AI开发的打包应用或解决方案，也要直接操作底层原语——无论是通过API还是聊天界面使用模型。你需要真正把它们推向极限。因为只有这样，你才能真正理解这些新“食材”的价值。这就像厨师获得了令人惊叹的新食材，但必须先熟悉它们，才能将它们融入新菜式中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And we had Dan Shipper on the podcast, he runs this newsletter and podcast to product a company called Every. And they work with companies to help them become more AI successful and adopt AI and all that stuff. And I asked him, what's the signal that a company will have success adopting AI and seeing huge productivity gains? And he said, does the CEO use ChatGPT or Claude daily?
turns.zh: 我们在播客上邀请了Dan Shipper，他负责为一家名为Every的公司运营新闻通讯和播客，帮助企业成功应用AI并实现生产力提升。我问他，如何判断一家公司在应用AI并获得巨大生产力提升方面是否成功？他说，CEO是否每天使用ChatGPT或Claude？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I feel like you're describing exactly, hourly,
turns.zh: 我觉得你描述的正是每小时的使用情况。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Literally hourly, or you could even have a measure of inference costs, right? Like the equivalent underlying inference compute cycles, right?
turns.zh: 确切地说，每小时的使用情况，甚至可以衡量推理成本，对吧？比如等效的底层推理计算周期，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many tokens you use?
turns.zh: 你使用了多少个Token？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I'm proud to say I am pretty sure I'm still the ... I just checked this recently, but I take pride in being the number one most expensive in inference cost user of Airtable AI, not just within our own company, but I think for a long time I was globally across all our customers vault. I mean, I'm extremely intentionally wasteful. Wasteful in the sense of I'll do something that costs maybe hundreds of dollars of actual inference costs. For instance, doing a lot of LLM calls against long transcripts of let's say, sales calls to extract different types of insights like here's the product apps, identify or here's summaries, et cetera. (00:14:49): And we also have now a capability that's basically like an LLM map reduce. So effectively, even if you can't fit the entire corpus of content into one LLM call, because the context window limitations, we'll map through all of this content and break it up into chunks and then perform an LLM call on each one and then perform an aggregation LLM call on those chunks. Very expensive, because you're basically running a highly expensive model against a lot of data and then running it again on the aggregates of that. But for me, hundreds of dollars spent on this exercise is trivial compared to the potential strategic value of having better insights. (00:15:29): It's as if a really, really smart chief of staff has gone through and read every single sales call transcript that we've had in the past year and giving me very astute product insights, marketing insights, kind of positioning insights and segmentation insights. That's invaluable. You could pay a consulting firm literally millions of dollars to get that quality of work. So to me, I still think the value versus the actual cost of AI when applied greedily but smartly, it's a crazy ratio. And more people should be aggressively throwing compute cycles at these very high value problems.
turns.zh:
是啊，我是说，我很自豪地说，我几乎可以肯定自己仍是 Airtable AI 推理成本使用量最大的用户——不仅在我们公司内部如此，而且在全球所有客户中长期保持着这一纪录。我是说，我故意浪费资源。所谓浪费，是指我会去做一些可能耗费数百美元实际推理成本的事情。比如，对销售通话的冗长转录文本进行大量 LLM 调用，以提取不同类型的洞察，比如产品应用情况、客户身份识别或摘要总结等。

（00:14:49）：我们现在还拥有一种类似 LLM 映射归约的功能。即便由于上下文窗口限制，无法将全部内容一次性输入 LLM 模型，我们也会将所有内容拆分成小块，分别进行 LLM 调用，并对这些小块执行聚合式 LLM 调用。这成本极高，因为你本质上是在对大量数据运行高昂的模型，然后再对其聚合结果重复调用。但对我来说，为此花费数百美元简直微不足道，与获取优质洞察所带来的潜在战略价值相比，这完全值得。

（00:15:29）：这就好像一位极其聪明的幕僚长仔细阅读了我们过去一年的所有销售通话记录，为我提供了极具洞察力的产品策略、市场营销、定位和细分见解。这些价值无可估量。若花数百万美元请咨询公司获取同等质量的洞察，那简直是天价。因此，我始终认为，在合理且谨慎地应用 AI 时，其价值与实际成本的比例简直令人惊叹。更多人应该积极将计算资源投入到这些高价值问题中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Until somebody tweets how you're costing the company so much on AI compute and you guys are going to be underwater.
turns.zh: 直到有人在推特上说你让公司在 AI 计算上花费巨大，公司要因此陷入财务危机了。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I'm just kidding. It's like how we have personally taken down the cashflow profile of the business.
turns.zh: 我开玩笑的。这就像我们亲手打破了公司的现金流曲线一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So CEO's, founders hearing this, they're probably like, okay, I should probably start doing this. What does this actually look like? I imagine you still have a lot of other stuff you got going on once, you got all these ... How do you change your day to day to do this?
turns.zh: 所以，各位 CEO 和创始人听到这些，可能就会想，嗯，我或许也该这么做了。但具体该怎么做呢？我猜你们日常还有很多其他事情要处理，一旦开始做这些事……该如何调整日常工作来实现这一目标呢？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, so I actually cut my one-on-one roster by default, and the idea is not that I don't want to spend time one-on-one with people, but rather that I found that the ... Just having more standing one-on-ones actually precludes me from engaging in more timely topics. I like to think of the best types of meetings as very urgency driven. And there's some timely topic, you've discovered some insight. Maybe I talked to some new startup and I learned something from their product or their approach. (00:17:20): And I want to bring that into how we're thinking about a new feature at Airtable or even just plant the seed with some different EPD people within Airtable, I want to make most meetings very timely and very informed by real alpha. There's got to be some kind of value and insight to seed that with. Now, in addition to that, I'll supplement with, when I'm in person with someone, I want to carve out time for a proper catch up and less structured, less timely, and just more of building a relationship with a human. (00:17:53): But I actually find that having that common .. It's almost a barbell approach where it's like if you're going to spend time with somebody in a freeform way, actually do it in a high quality, not forced weekly ritual way. Go for a longer lunch or coffee walk or whatever in person when you can. Maybe that's a once every month or two kind of thing. And then the in-betweens are either topical, so we do have standing meetings for ... Now, we have a weekly basically sprint check-in on all of our AI execution stuff, which now is half the company or half the EPD org is working on AI capabilities. (00:18:29): We're trying to ship very quickly, like I basically want to always ask the question, how would an AI native company, like a cursor or windsurf, et cetera, how would they execute? And are we executing as fast as them and taking advantage of all the new stuff as well as them? So bringing that level of intensity and urgency to how I spend my time within, that's been the biggest shift for me.
turns.zh: 是的，我实际上默认削减了我的单对单会议安排。这么做并不是因为我不想花时间与人进行一对一交流，而是因为我发现……过多的固定一对一会议反而会妨碍我探讨更及时的话题。我认为最理想的会议类型应该是由紧迫性驱动的。比如，当你发现某个新洞察，或者与某家初创公司交流后学到新产品或策略时，我希望能将这些见解融入我们在 Airtable 开发新功能的思考中，或者至少在 Airtable 内部与不同部门的同事种下这些想法的种子。我希望大多数会议都紧扣当下议题，基于真实的早期产品反馈提供有价值的见解。除此之外，当我与某人面对面时，我会专门留出时间进行深入交流，减少形式化和时间压力，更多地去建立人际关系。（00:17:20）但我发现这种平衡很重要……这就像杠铃策略——如果你要以自由形式与人交流，就要确保质量高，而不是强制每周固定仪式。当条件允许时，可以安排更长时间的午餐或咖啡漫谈，保持每月一两次的频率。其余时间则聚焦于专题讨论，比如我们每周都会召开关于人工智能执行进展的会议，目前全公司或工程开发部一半团队都在致力于人工智能能力的研发。（00:18:29）我们力求快速交付成果，比如我总会问：像 Cursor 或 Windsurf 这样的专注人工智能的公司，他们是如何执行的？我们是否能像他们一样高效，充分利用所有新技术？将这种紧迫感和高效性融入我的日常安排，才是我最大的转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a change you've made to help the company move faster and match that sort of pace?
turns.zh: 你为帮助公司更快发展、跟上这种节奏做过哪些改变？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, we did do a reorg of the EPD org. So before we had ... we've gone through a few different reorgs over the past, call it, four years. The original state as we just proliferated, I think by default or incrementally, was that we had a bunch of groups that were each responsible for a feature or a surface area. So there was a group responsible for search within our table, and there was a group responsible for mobile experience and so on and so forth. And that has its benefits. Obviously, that team can go and get really ramped up on that part of the code base, that part of the product. (00:19:36): But it has the disadvantage of yeah, you tend to think incrementally when everyone's remit is actually a feature that they incrementally improve by definition as opposed to thinking about a mission or a outcome goal that might need to coordinate dramatic changes across a wider set of surface areas instead of just each one incrementally improving. And so, we reorged initially to basically different business units effectively. So I know Airbnb has done the functional to GM back, et cetera. This was more like saying, "Look, we have an enterprise business" and them MO there is more about scalability. (00:20:19): Can we support the larger scale data sets and use cases? Do you have the core capabilities needed to be able to push out an app to maybe 10,000 seats or 20,000 seats for product operations? A lot of architecture, a lot of scale, that kind of work. We would have, what we call the teams filler, which is more about self-serve, kind of the product UX, how easy it is to adopt the product on board, share, do all the kind of basic functionality. An AI pillar, solutions pillar, and basically infra. And what we found though with that approach is that there was still ... there was more kind of holistic bets being made. (00:20:58): So the team's pillar could think not just about one feature, but the overall onboarding experience where really about Nuxt in a way that touched multiple parts of the product, but it still felt like it wasn't ... Especially as we started to execute more on AI stuff, it wasn't allowing us to aggressively and quickly move as a AI native company would. I mean, when you look at the cursors of the world, they're shipping major new stuff every week. And it's not like, "Oh, well we have this separate roadmap for enterprise, we have this roadmap for this group." (00:21:33): And it just feels like one cohesive product that's shipping at a breakneck pace. So we did this recent reorg where now we have what I call the fast thinking group, which officially is called AI platform, but it really means we want to just ship a bunch of new capabilities on a near weekly basis. And each of them should be truly awesome value. You should drop your jaw, how awesome it is to use this new capability in Airtable. And then separately, we have the slow thinking group, and that's not meant to be better or worse. It's literally like you need fast and slow thinking in the common sense to operate as a human.
turns.zh:
是的。我的意思是，我们确实对EPD部门进行了重组。在过去四年左右的时间里，我们经历了多次不同的重组。最初的状态是，我们只是随意或逐步扩张，各个团队各自负责某个功能或产品领域。比如，有个团队负责表格内的搜索功能，还有个团队负责移动端体验等等。这种模式有其优势——显然，这些团队能够专注于代码库的某个部分或产品模块。但它也有弊端，即团队往往会以渐进式思维为主，因为每个人的职责实际上都是对某个功能进行逐步改进，而非从更宏观的角度去思考任务或目标，比如如何通过协调多个领域的重大变革来实现产品使命或最终结果。

因此，我们最初的重组实质上是将业务单元进行了有效拆分。我知道Airbnb也将功能型团队转回了集团管理层等。这次重组更像是在说：“看，我们有了一个企业级业务”，而其核心在于可扩展性——我们能否支持更大规模的数据集和用例？你是否具备将应用推向1万或2万用户所需的核心能力？这涉及大量架构优化和规模扩展工作。我们还组建了所谓的“团队填充组”，主要负责自助式服务，比如产品用户体验、产品上线便利性等；设立了AI支柱、解决方案支柱以及基础设施团队。

但我们发现，这种架构仍存在局限——团队往往只能专注于单个功能，而非整体产品体验。例如，某个团队可能只负责Nuxt相关功能，却触及产品多个模块，但仍缺乏整体协同感。尤其是在AI战略推进过程中，我们未能像AI原生公司那样高效快速地创新。看看全球科技巨头，他们每周都能推出重大创新成果。而我们却被迫分开管理企业和产品路线图，仿佛两个独立的公司。

因此，我们进行了最新重组，成立了所谓的“快速思考组”，正式命名为AI平台，但实质上是希望每周都能推出多项创新功能，每项功能都必须具备令人惊叹的价值。比如，在Airtable中使用新功能时，你会惊呼“太棒了”。同时，我们还保留了“慢思考组”，这里没有优劣之分，就像常识中需要快速和慢速思考来维持人类的正常运转一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have that book behind me.
turns.zh: 我身后有那本书。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, I love that book. But slow thinking it's like, it's just a different mode of planning and executing, right? It's like more deliberate that require more premeditation. We can't just ship a new piece of infrastructure that has a lot of data complexity like our data store HyperDB that now can handle multi-hundred million record data sets. That's not something you ship in a week in a hacky prototype. So we now have these two separate parts of the company, and I actually think what's really cool is they actually compliment each other very well, right? (00:22:46): Because the fast execution, the AI stuff, that creates the top of funnel excitement that also inspires new use cases and new users to come to Airtable, including in large enterprise, right? Enterprises can use this stuff too. It's not just like a SMB thing, but the slow thinking basically allows those initial seeds of adoption to Sprout and grow into much larger deployments. Whereas I think a lot of the challenge for many of the AI native companies I've seen is that they could have a very wide top of funnel, like get all of this AI, tourist traffic. (00:23:19): A lot of interest, a lot of early usage, but then sometimes the challenge is how do you turn that into more durable growth and get each of those adoption seeds to retain and expand over time.
turns.zh: 是啊，我超爱那本书。不过“慢思考”其实就是一种不同的规划和执行模式，对吧？它更讲究深思熟虑，需要更充分的预先策划。我们不可能在一周内就发布一个像HyperDB这样数据复杂度极高的基础设施产品，它现在已经能处理数亿条数据记录了。这可不是能用一周时间拼凑出的原型产品。所以我们现在把公司分成了两个独立的部门，我觉得最妙的是它们能相互补充，对吧？（00:22:46）因为快速执行、人工智能相关的业务能激发用户的兴趣，也能为Airtable带来新的应用场景和新用户，甚至能渗透到大型企业中——毕竟企业也能用这些技术，又不只是中小企业的专属。但慢思考模式能让最初的用户种子发芽成长为大规模部署。反观我见过的许多专注人工智能的公司，挑战往往在于它们虽然能吸引大量初期用户，但之后就难以转化为可持续的增长，无法让这些用户种子长期留存并扩展规模。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. I've never heard of this way of structuring teams, the fast thinking, thinking fast, thinking slow, the Kahneman. It's so interesting for the fast thinking team, do you find there's specific archetypes of people that are successful there? Is it a lot of bringing in new people that are not just used to the way of working at our table? What do you find?
turns.zh: 这太酷了。我从没听说过这种团队结构方式——快思考、快速决策、慢思考，还有卡尼曼的理论。快思考团队里有没有特定的成功人格模型？是不是需要引入很多不习惯我们公司工作方式的新人？你有什么发现？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: We have a mix. So we brought in ... I mean, we're always hiring, right? There was never a point in the company's life where we stopped hiring. And candidly, even when we had to do two rifts, that's significantly reduced our head count. We had just way too quickly grown and overscaled the business at a certain point. But even when we did our rifts, we were still actively recruiting and hiring in ... I mean every major department, but especially in EPD, because it's always been my belief that it would be arrogant to say that we have all the people we ever need already in the roster today, right? (00:24:29): We're always going to need to find new, fresh perspectives, new skillsets, et cetera. And so, we've continued to hire ... I think we've learned as we've gone along of what is the ideal type of hire, and we've done some actual hires and learned from that as well. But I think the fast thinking part, it really just requires a lot of ... Somebody who's able to operate with a lot of autonomy, who's entrepreneurial in nature. Now, it doesn't mean they have to literally be a former founder. I know some companies are, like Rippling for instance, does a lot of actual acquisitions and gets actual founders into the company. (00:25:04): We found that that's great and we've done some of that as well. But also there are some really, really capable people who we didn't literally have to acquire in, and yet, they're just able to think full stack about the problem and the user experience. Problem, not just meaning the technical layers of the problem, but also, what is the wow factor we're trying to create. So tangibly we're doing this new thing that's about to ship, where not only can you describe the app you want to build and then iterate on it with our conversational agent Omni. (00:25:41): And it builds it with the existing air table platform capabilities, but we're also giving it the ability to actually do code gen, to extend those apps with really final mile very bespoke functionality or visuals. So you could say, "Hey, generate me a very, very specific type of map view with this kind of heat mapping and this kind of icons and ..."
turns.zh: 我们的团队成员背景各异。所以我们一直在招人……我说的是，我们一直在招聘，对吧？公司从成立到现在，从来没有停止过招聘。说实话，即使我们经历了两次裁员，也大大削减了员工规模。但即便在裁员期间，我们仍在积极招聘，尤其是在各个主要部门，尤其是EPD部门，因为我一直认为，如果我们自视清高地认为现有团队已能满足所有需求，那未免太自大了。（00:24:29）我们永远需要寻找新视角、新技能等人才。在这个过程中，我们逐渐摸索出理想的招聘标准，也通过实际招聘积累了经验。但关键在于，我们需要能独立运作、具有创业精神的人才。这并不意味着他们必须是前创业者——比如Rippling公司就通过大量收购引入了创始人团队，我们也尝试过这种模式。但我们也发现，有些能力出众的人无需收购就能融入团队，他们能全方位思考问题和用户体验。问题不止于技术层面，还包括我们要打造的惊喜体验。比如即将上线的全新产品，你不仅能描述想要构建的应用，还能借助我们的对话式智能助手Omni进行迭代。（00:25:04）该产品基于现有Air Table平台功能构建，同时支持代码生成，用于扩展应用的最后一公里定制功能或视觉效果。比如你可以说：“用这个热力图和图标生成特定类型的地图视图……”

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: It's kind of like heat mapping and this kind of icons. And when you click it, do this. And that's a capability that there's so much ambiguity in some of the design decisions around it. And you have to blend that design thinking with some of the technical constraints of what can the AI models actually one shot effectively? (00:26:21): And if not, how do you add in the right human workflow for approval and review, and the reprompting and so on? So just so many different design decisions, and you need somebody who can really think full-stack about that kind of product and is not overwhelmed by that kind of open-endedness, but relishes in it.
turns.zh: 这就像热力图和图标。当用户点击时，还能执行特定操作。围绕这些设计决策存在诸多不确定性，你必须将设计思维与技术约束相结合——比如AI模型能否有效一次性完成任务？如果不行，又该如何补充合适的人工流程进行审批、审核、再提示等环节？如此多的设计决策，需要能全方位思考产品的候选人，而非被开放性难题压垮，而是乐在其中。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I will say just as a note, I consider myself at my core a product UX person. That's my passion. And everything else I've had to learn to run this company is almost like what was a necessary part of the journey. But my real passion is thinking about product UX. And I think of UX in a deeper sense than just the cosmetic design. What you could put into a framer kind of prototype. I think of it as literally what should this product do and how should it represent that and behave for the user? That is the product, in my opinion, right. And of course, then you have to figure out technically what's possible and how to implement it. (00:27:36): But I think to me what's under executed today in the world of AI products is there's so many awesome capabilities of AI, and most of them are really under merchandise, and there's very poor, actually, visual or otherwise metaphors or affordances given to users to help represent or understand what those underlying capabilities are. I mean, ChatGPT obviously extremely successful product, so not knocking it at all, but you come in and you just get this completely blank chat box by default, and now they have suggestions underneath and so on. (00:28:13): But the product UX part of me is just craving more visual metaphors or colors or some kind of use the canvas of a web interface and all the richness interaction you create there to better represent or show all the different things that you can do with the underlying model, right. And so that's something we've tried to do with Airtable, is show all of the different states and use colors even to play those up.
turns.zh:
顺便说一句，我认为自己本质上是一名产品用户体验设计师。这是我的热情所在。为了运营这家公司，我不得不学习的其他一切技能，几乎都是旅程中必不可少的部分。但我真正的热情在于思考产品用户体验。我对用户体验的理解比单纯的表面设计要深刻得多——比如在 Framer 里制作原型时所考虑的那些。我所思考的是：这个产品应该做什么，应该如何为用户呈现这些功能并提供交互体验？在我看来，这才是一款产品。当然，之后你还得从技术层面思考哪些功能是可行的，以及如何实现它们。  
（00:27:36）：但在我看来，当下人工智能产品领域存在一个被低估的问题——AI 拥有许多强大的功能，但大多数产品都未能充分利用这些功能。用户得到的视觉或其他隐喻或交互提示非常有限，难以理解底层技术的运作方式。比如 ChatGPT 显然是一款极其成功的产品，我绝不是在贬低它，但默认情况下用户看到的只是一个空白的聊天框，现在他们才添加了建议功能等提示。  
（00:28:13）：但我对产品用户体验的执着在于渴望更多视觉隐喻、色彩，或是利用网页界面的画布及其丰富的交互功能，更好地呈现或展示底层模型所能实现的各种功能。这正是我们在 Airtable 上努力做的事情——展示所有不同状态，甚至用颜色来突出这些状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how much of this connects with I just had Nick Turley on the podcast. He's head of ChatGPT at OpenAI, and he had these two really interesting insights that resonate directly with what you're describing. One is he has this concept of whenever something is being worked on, he's always asking, " Is this maximally accelerated? How do we move faster? If this is important, what would allow us to move faster?"
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这与我最近邀请到播客上的尼克·特利（Nick Turley）的观点有很多共鸣。他是 OpenAI 的 ChatGPT 负责人，他提出了两个非常有趣的见解，与你所描述的直接相关。其中一个是，每当开发某项功能时，他总会问：“这是否能最大限度地加速进程？我们如何加快速度？如果这很重要，怎样才能加快进度？”

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love that that's one of the themes that's coming up as you talk, is just this creating this very clear sense of speed. And you even call it the fast-thinking team, like, "You are going to move fast." And then the other one is just this insight that with AI, you often don't know what it can do and what people want to do with it until it's out. So there's this need to get it out, and that'll tell you what it should be.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你谈话中反复提到的两个主题：一是营造一种清晰的速度感；二是关于人工智能的洞察——在产品推出之前，你往往不知道它能做什么，用户想用它来做什么。因此，必须尽快推出产品，这样才能发现真正的需求。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I couldn't agree more with both of those, and particularly on the second point, I think it's interesting. Clearly, there have been companies that have both been successful in PLG and more sales-led distribution for AI products. The most notable ones I can think of are Palantir with their AIP deployments. That's obviously very sales-led. You're not PLG into a Palantir deployment. But even companies like Harvey and so on, they're doing very well. And it's primarily, from what I understand, sales-led. (00:29:59): You're not self- serving into a Harvey instance at a law firm. And yet, to me, the best way to get AI value out there is experientially, right. And so you can kind of get that in a sales motion. You can show a demo. Maybe you can do a POC, but it's so much more powerful when you just open up the doors and say, "Anyone who wants to come and sign up and trial this product can." And I think to me, it's a real proof point that ChatGPT is arguably the most successful kind of PLG product of all time, just in terms of sheer scale of users. Like they announced 700 million... Is it MAUs or week... I think it's actually-
turns.zh: 关于这两点，我完全赞同，尤其是第二点，我觉得很有意思。显然，有些公司在人工智能产品的PLG（产品生命周期）和以销售为主导的分销模式上都取得了成功。我能想到的最典型例子是Palantir的AIP（应用集成平台）部署——这显然是以销售为主导的。你不可能通过PLG方式将AIP部署到Palantir的客户那里。但即便像Harvey这样的公司，他们也做得非常出色。据我所知，这些公司主要还是以销售为主导的。（00:29:59）你不可能在律师事务所将Harvey实例作为自用产品推销。然而在我看来，让AI价值真正落地的最佳方式是通过体验式推广。通过销售演示、POC（概念验证）等方式固然有效，但当你真正敞开大门，宣布“欢迎任何想来体验这款产品的用户”时，效果要强得多。我认为ChatGPT可以说是史上最成功的PLG产品，这从其用户规模上就可见一斑。他们声称有7亿用户……是MAU（月活跃用户）还是周活？……应该是周活吧。

turns.en: Weekly active users.
turns.zh: 周活用户。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Weekly.
turns.zh: 每周活跃用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 10% of humans on earth use it-
turns.zh: 全球10%的人口在使用它——

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: That's insane.
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... weekly.
turns.zh: ……每周活跃用户。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: That's insane. In how many years? A few years.
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。用了多少年？几年吧。

turns.en: Three years. Under three years.

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. So I mean, literally, that is just the most insane ramp curve. And I don't think they would've gotten there if you couldn't just come in and literally try the product out. And as a little bit of a rebuttal of the point I made earlier where I think ChatGPT doesn't do a ton right now, and even earlier they did even less to expose all the different ways you could use it, but they just made it so frictionless to just try it for yourself that you as a user could come in and just literally ask it anything and see how it did. And of course, people in the early days tried to stump it and showed, "Oh look, see, it's not that smart. It doesn't answer this hard question really well." (00:31:26): But clearly, the magical nature of it still appealed to you enough. Everybody used it. And so I think I do have a view. We've gone through that whole arc of we started PLG. I'd like to think Airtable was one of the PLG darlings of our era. And anyway, I started moving up market and doing more sales execution, although that was still always on top of usually PLG within an enterprise, but we started doing more and more sales execution. We still have that. That's still really important for our business. But I also think, me personally, one of my goals is to shift my attention back into that kind of builder-led adoption and literally showing in the product experientially, not telling in a deck, the value that you can get from AI and Airtable. (00:32:20): I think that's so key, and it's [inaudible 00:32:23], but it's also more than that. It's not just literally how do you onboard somebody into the product. It's literally thinking about the entire product experience itself, right. And in our case, we just made the entire product experience AI-centric. It used to be that we had kind of this secondary thing that you could ask questions to the assistant sidebar. We now made our agent the default way of doing everything in Airtable, and it's now the Airtable app, as you know, it is almost like an artifact that's manipulated by and can be tool used by the agent.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，简直太疯狂了，这升坡曲线简直不可思议。我觉得如果用户不能亲自试用产品，他们根本不可能达到现在的效果。这也反驳了我之前提到的观点，即ChatGPT目前做得还不够，甚至早期他们更不愿意展示产品可以应用的各种场景，但他们让用户能够无障碍地亲自尝试，让用户可以随意提问并观察结果。当然，早期有些人试图难倒它，证明“看吧，它并不聪明，对这个难题回答得也不好”。（00:31:26）但显然，它的神奇之处还是吸引了大家。每个人都在用它。所以我确实有一些看法。我们经历了整个PLG（产品生命周期）的过程。我认为Airtable是我们这个时代PLG的典范。无论如何，我开始向市场上游进军，加强销售执行，虽然这仍然主要是在企业内部进行PLG，但我们开始做越来越多的销售执行工作。我们现在依然在做这件事。这对我们的业务仍然非常重要。但我个人认为，我的目标之一是将注意力重新转向以用户为主导的采用，真正通过产品体验而非演示文稿来展示AI和Airtable能带来的价值。（00:32:20）我认为这非常关键，[00:32:23未听清]，但不止于此。这不仅仅是如何让用户上手产品，而是要从整体产品体验出发。在我们的案例中，我们把整个产品体验都以AI为核心。过去，用户可以通过侧边栏的助手功能提问，但现在我们把智能助手作为Airtable所有操作的默认方式。如今的Airtable应用，几乎就像一个由智能助手操控并可供用户使用的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow that thread. So if you go to Airtable.com today, it looks like basically all the other AI app building sites. Now it's just tell me what you want to build. Thoughts on that, as just a thing everyone's starting to do is there... what do you think comes next? Is this... Is it working well?
turns.zh: 让我接着说这个话题。如果你今天访问Airtable.com，它看起来和其他AI应用搭建网站基本一样。现在就是告诉你想搭建什么。关于这一点，你怎么看？毕竟这已经成为大家都在做的事情...你觉得接下来会怎样？这样做效果好吗？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: There's clearly an incredible magic to vibe coding and app building with AI. And this is actually a prime illustration in my view of that concept we talked about a second ago, which is as capabilities of these underlying models evolve, the form factor in the product UX also needs to evolve with it. And so the earliest models, like the kind of original ChatGPT, like GPT-3.5 kind of era models were not nearly as smart as the current models. And so you couldn't really ask it to one shot a more complicated chunk of code, or certainly not like a full stack app, and expect it to work. (00:33:56): And so the right form factor for leveraging those models in a software creation context was GitHub Copilot, right. It's like auto-complete a few lines of code at a time. But you couldn't chat to it and tell it, "Build me this entire app from scratch." And I think that as the models got better and better, you saw that the new form factors emerge. I think Cursor did a great job of being an early pioneer of this more age agentic way of leveraging the models to do more complex things and generate more larger chunks of code. (00:34:27): And now with Composer, you can literally just go into Cursor and build an app from scratch, build me a 3D shooter game from scratch, and just watch it go and create all the files and fill out each file, and then the thing actually runs some of the time. And so to me, this is where the world is going. The models are clearly getting smarter. And if you think about the original vision of Airtable, it was always about democratizing software creation. We just strongly believed that the number of people who use apps far outweighs the number of people who can actually build their own or manipulate apps and harness custom software to their advantage.
turns.zh: 显然，与AI一起编写代码和开发应用程序存在着令人惊叹的魔力。在我看来，这恰恰印证了我们刚刚讨论的那个概念——随着底层模型的能力不断提升，产品用户体验的设计也必须与之同步进化。最早的模型，比如原始的ChatGPT、GPT-3.5时代的模型，其智能程度远不及当前的模型。因此，你无法指望它能一口气完成一段复杂的代码，更别说开发一个完整的全栈应用程序了。（00:33:56）所以，在软件开发场景中利用这些模型的合适形式是GitHub Copilot，它能一次性自动补全几行代码。但你无法对它说：“从零开始给我开发整个应用程序。”随着模型性能的不断提升，我们见证了新形式的应用诞生。Cursor就很好地诠释了这种以更具代理性的方式利用模型完成更复杂任务、生成更大代码块的先锋理念。（00:34:27）而现在有了Composer，你甚至可以直接在Cursor中从零开发一个应用程序，比如创建一个3D射击游戏，看着它自动生成所有文件并运行起来。这在我看来，正是未来的发展方向。模型的智能程度无疑在不断提升。如果回顾Airtable最初的愿景，那就是让软件开发民主化。我们坚信，使用应用程序的人数远远超过能够自主开发、修改应用程序并利用定制软件为自己创造价值的人数。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds very familiar, very familiar these days.
turns.zh: 这听起来很熟悉，现在确实很常见。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And so I think this is, it's a different means to the same end. And so it's almost like we have to lean into this because if we started Airtable today, this is what we would be all in on. Now I think that the advantage that we have, and I do think you have to be realistic to yourself, especially as a company that predates GenAI and now has to find your new footing in the AI landscape. You can't fool yourself and just say like, "Okay, I'm going to throw in some AI stuff on the landing... on the marketing site, put in a couple AI features, and call it a day." (00:35:43): I think you actually have to take a clean slate approach to saying, "How would our mission best be expressed? If you were literally founding a new company from scratch with the same mission, how would you execute on that mission using a fully AI native approach?" And then, by the way, do you have useful building blocks that you can leverage from your existing product and your existing business, or are you literally worse off having this legacy asset versus starting something from scratch? And I don't think the answer is always yes or no. I think it just depends on the product. (00:36:19): And if you can't really introspect and say, "Look, I think I'm better off doing this with the pieces that I have for my existing business and product," then I think you should sell. You should find a buyer for that company and then go. And if you really care about this mission, go and start the next carnation of it. In my case, I really thought about this and really feel strongly that the building blocks that we have, these no code components, actually do allow us to execute better on this vision than if I had to start from scratch. (00:36:50): Meaning the problem with vibe coding, especially if we're building business apps... So I should clarify that we want to democratize software creation, but specifically, we are focused on business apps. We're not trying to be the platform where you create a cool viral consumer game. This is for like your CRM, right. Or if you want to build an inventory management system as a small restaurant or a lawyer trying to build a case management system, that's what we've always been focused on. And I think in this AI-native world, clearly, you should be able to generate those apps agentically. (00:37:24): And yet if you have an agent that has to generate every single bit of that app from scratch, from code, it's going to be very unreliable. There's going to be bugs. There's going to be data and security issues. And then you're also going to have a context collapse, as it just cannot manage all of the code that it's written, basically, as the app gets more and more complex. And what we actually have are basically these primitives that the agent can manipulate and use without having to literally write the code from scratch to represent, "Here's a beautiful crud interface on top of the data layer. (00:37:57): Ours is real-time and collaborative, and really rich, and has collaboration on it. And by the way, here's all these other view types and a layout engine for a custom interface, a layout, or automations and business logic." And so it's almost like in programming terms, the Airtable pieces in our Lego kit today can be used by this agent as almost like a more expressive DSL, like a domain-specific language to build business apps instead of literally having to write everything down to the SQL and HTML and JavaScript to build every part of that app from scratch. (00:38:31): And so if we can combine the best of both worlds, we have these very reliable, high-quality Lego pieces. Now, an agent can go and assemble them for you instead of you just using the GUI to do that. And by the way, if you do want to fall back to the GUI, there's a really great kind of way for the non-technical user to still understand and participate in what's going on. Whereas if you're not technical, you can't inspect the code underneath a v0 or Lovable or Revolut app, right. (00:38:58): It's just kind of opaque to you. And if you can't re- prop it to get what you want, you're kind of stuck. This is much more akin to a developer using Cursor can generate lots of code, but then can still drop back to the IDE to edit and manipulate it to the final production-ready state. So that's kind of the play that we're making. And if I didn't fully and truly believe we have a better shot at doing it with our existing product, I wouldn't be running this company in its form today.
turns.zh:
是啊，没错。我觉得这不过是殊途同归。说白了，我们必须全力以赴，因为如果我们今天才创立Airtable公司，肯定会一心一意地专注于此。现在我认为，我们面临的挑战在于——我觉得你必须对自己保持清醒的认识，尤其是对于一家先于GenAI问世、如今又必须在AI领域重新站稳脚跟的公司来说。你不能自欺欺人，比如说"好吧，我在登陆页面加点AI功能，营销网站上放几个AI模块，就大功告成了"。（00:35:43）：我认为你必须采取全新的方法，问自己："如何才能最有效地传递我们的使命？如果从零开始创立一家拥有相同使命的新公司，你会如何利用全AI原生技术来实现这一目标？"顺便说一句，你是否能从现有产品和业务中借鉴有用的组件，还是说相较于从零开始，这些遗留资产反而会拖后腿？我认为答案不一定是肯定或否定。这完全取决于产品本身。（00:36:19）：如果你无法深入反思，坦言"看，我觉得用现有业务和产品的组件更划算"，那么我建议你应该卖掉公司，寻找买家，然后重新出发。如果你真心认同这个使命，那就去开创新的篇章。就我个人而言，我深思熟虑后坚信，我们现有的组件——这些无代码组件——确实能比从零开始更有效地实现我们的愿景。（00:36:50）：说到无代码开发，尤其是用于商业应用时……这里我要澄清一点，我们致力于让软件开发民主化，但具体来说，我们专注于商业应用。我们无意打造能开发酷炫病毒式消费者游戏的平台，而是面向CRM系统、餐厅的小型库存管理系统，或者律师的案件管理系统等场景。（00:37:24）：在AI原生世界里，显然你应该能自主生成这些应用。但如果让智能体从零开始编写每一行代码，那可靠性堪忧，必然会出现漏洞、数据和安全问题。随着应用日益复杂，智能体还会面临上下文崩溃的问题，根本无法管理所有编写的代码。而我们现有的组件本质上是智能体可以操作和使用的原始模块，无需从零编写代码。比如："在数据层之上构建一个美观的CRUD界面"。我们的系统实时协作、功能丰富，支持协作功能。此外，还有各种视图类型、布局引擎用于自定义界面、自动化流程和业务逻辑。（00:38:31）：所以用编程术语来说，如今Airtable套件中的积木，可以被智能体当作更具表达力的DSL（领域特定语言），用于构建商业应用，而无需从头开始编写SQL、HTML和JavaScript代码。（00:39:04）：如果我们能将两者优势结合起来，就能实现最佳效果。
可靠、高质量的乐高积件。现在，代理人可以替您进行组装，而无需您直接使用图形用户界面（GUI）来完成此操作。顺便说一句，如果您确实想回归到GUI界面，对于非技术用户而言，仍有一种非常棒的方式来理解并参与整个过程。相反，如果您不具备技术背景，就无法查看V0、Lovable或Revolut应用程序底层的代码，对吧（00:38:58）？这对您来说简直是神秘莫测的。如果您无法通过重新配置来获取所需功能，那就只能束手无策了。这与开发者使用Cursor生成大量代码，然后再回到集成开发环境（IDE）中进行编辑和调整，最终生成可投入生产的代码非常相似。这正是我们正在努力实现的目标。如果我不完全相信凭借现有产品就能更好地实现这一目标，我绝不会以今天的形式经营这家公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm talking to a lot of founders that are going through the journey are going on, which is, "We've had a business for a decade, AI emerged, and wow, we got to figure out something that works... that could work even better." And so I'm trying to pull out the threads that are consistently working across these journeys because I think a lot of companies are trying to figure this out. So one that you just touched on is just if you were to start today, what will you do? (00:39:48): What would that business be? Plus, how can... do we have an unfair advantage with the thing we've done in the past? That feels like an important ingredient. And then the other... circling back to stuff you've shared already, there's just creating a sense of urgency and pace and getting people to understand this is how things move in AI, and we need to create this fast-thinking team. I love that metaphor in framing. (00:40:11): And then there's the point you made about just talking to AI regularly as the founder feels like an important element, just like to truly be this ICCO talking to AI, working with AI regularly. Just on that note a little bit more, just to give people a sense of what this looks like day to day. So you're talking to Omni all day trying to and undertook... flex the power of what you can do and iterate on it. Is there anything else you're doing day to day that helps you figure out what to do for the business?
turns.zh: 我与许多正在经历创业历程的创始人交流，他们面临着这样一个问题："我们经营企业十年，人工智能兴起后，哇，我们得想办法做出有效的解决方案……甚至能做得更好"。因此，我试图从这些历程中提炼出始终有效的思路，因为我相信许多公司都在努力解决这个难题。刚才你提到的关键问题是，如果你从今天开始创业，你会怎么做？（00:39:48）：你的业务会是什么？此外，我们能否利用过去的经验获得竞争优势？这似乎是一个关键要素。还有其他方面……回到你之前分享的内容，营造紧迫感和节奏感，让人们明白这就是人工智能的发展规律，我们需要组建一支快速响应的团队。我很欣赏这种框架设计的比喻。（00:40:11）：你提到作为创始人，定期与人工智能对话也很重要，就像真正成为ICCO（人工智能首席创意官），定期与人工智能合作。再多说几句，让大家感受一下日常的工作状态。比如，你整天与Omni进行对话，尝试发挥其功能并进行迭代。还有哪些日常工作能帮助你为业务制定策略？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: One, I try to use as many different AI products, including not Airtable, as I can, and both literally for the novelty factor and just some new cool demo comes out. Like Runway release their immersive world engine, and so I'm going to go try it out. When Sesame AI put out their cool interactive voice chat demo, I tried that out because even though we don't have a direct and near-term need for really realistic and interruptible voice mode where it's not as core to our capabilities, I just want to understand and get a feel for everything that's out there. (00:41:23): And I try to invent little, almost like side projects of my own, to have a real reason to use these products. Like, "Oh, cool. What if I were to take... What if I were to try to create a funny little short... a funny video short using a combination of HeyGen avatars with a script, like a comical script generated by AI? And maybe it'll be on an interesting topic. So I'll do deep research on the topic with ChatGPT and pull together the results, have it compose kind of a little dialogue.
turns.zh: 首先，我尽可能多地尝试各种AI产品，包括非Airtable的产品，既是为了新鲜感，也是为了体验新兴的酷炫演示。比如Runway推出了沉浸式世界引擎，我就去尝试了。Sesame AI发布了酷炫的互动语音聊天演示，我也去体验了，尽管我们短期内没有直接需求，但我希望了解市场动态，感受各家产品的差异。（00:41:23）：我还会自己构思一些小项目，找到使用这些产品的理由。比如，"哦，真酷。如果我能用HeyGen虚拟形象结合AI生成的剧本，创作一个有趣的短视频会怎样？主题可以选个热点话题。先用ChatGPT深入研究，再整合结果，让它生成对话框架。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you actually do this? Is there something you made?
turns.zh: 你真的做过吗？有没有成果？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. That's literally an example of something, just a fun weekend project. And to be honest, these things only take you an hour if you become kind of pretty proficient with using the products. They're all so easy to use. You can literally do the deep research thing, kick off query, make a coffee, come back in 20 minutes. Okay, let me prompt it to generate me some dialogue. It's a little bit like what NotebookLM does for you out of the box, but sometimes I like to just do it myself. And then, okay, let me take the script and cut it up and turn it into a HeyGen avatar and then download the video and play it. (00:42:32): And just for fun. I'm not trying to make that into an actual YouTube video business. But I think coming up with these different fun weekend projects is a really useful construct to force myself to actually try these products in a more than just a Twitch click way. And what it gives me is, A, it's not just understanding the models, which is also very, very important, right. GPT-5 came out yesterday, and playing around with it a bunch just on a variety of different personal use cases, but there's a difference between just understanding the model but then also understanding the product form factors in which they can be placed, right. (00:43:15): Meaning when you apply the model in a more structured way, when you apply the model with different tool calling than maybe what ChatGPT has in its out-of-the-box form, when you apply it with a more agentic workflow, again, that might be different from what ChatGPT gives you out-of-the-box, that's when you kind of learn you really get to inspire yourself on what are the product's form factors that these new models can take. And plus, by the way, I find it to be really fun. There is to me a delight and entertainment value to just using AI, period, because A, it's not perfectly predictable. (00:43:57): So I think the element of you're not quite sure what you're going to get. It's like a box of chocolates. And B, it always blows my mind just to think about, "Wow, five years ago we didn't have any of this stuff." AI was like, okay, it's like we can do predictive analytics. There's some basically very advanced kind of regressions that we could run with AI, but it looked nothing like this in its current form, and it's just actually super fun, in my opinion, to get to play around with all the different types of products that come out. (00:44:33): I think that is a big part of it because on the point about the pace of the world moving so much faster in AI than any other landscape in SaaS, in the mature SaaS era, it was important to study your competition. If you were building a SaaS company, you'd be crazy not to follow Salesforce every year and see what the major releases they're putting out are, or ServiceNow, or so on. (00:45:03): This is the equivalent of that, but there's major new releases and products and so on every week, not every year. And so I just think you have to say abreast of all... of it all and combining this with our point earlier of a lot of this has to be experienced, not just read. You can't just read the write-up on TechCrunch or even a tweet about a new capability. You kind of have to try it to really get a sense of what it is.
turns.zh: 是啊。这确实是个例子，就是个有趣的周末项目。说实话，如果你对这些产品用得比较熟练的话，这些事情只需要一个小时就能完成。它们都非常易用。你可以深入研究，启动查询，做杯咖啡，20分钟后再回来。好吧，让我提示它生成一些对话。这有点像NotebookLM出厂时就能提供的功能，但有时我喜欢自己动手操作。然后，好的，我会拿走这个脚本，把它剪切成HeyGen的虚拟形象，再下载视频并播放。（00:42:32）：只是为了好玩。我不是想把它做成真正的YouTube视频业务。但我认为想出这些有趣的周末项目是一个非常有用的方法，能迫使自己以不仅仅是Twitch上随手点击的方式真正试用这些产品。它能给我带来两点好处：首先，不只是理解模型，这一点也非常重要，对吧。GPT-5昨天刚发布，我在各种个人用例上大量玩耍，但理解模型和理解产品形态是两回事，对吧。（00:43:15）：也就是说，当你以更有条理的方式应用模型，当你使用与ChatGPT出厂版本不同的工具调用方式，当你采用更具主动性的工作流程时，与ChatGPT出厂版本相比，这可能会有所不同。这时你会发现，你真的能启发自己，了解这些新模型可以应用于哪些产品形态。另外，顺便说一句，我觉得这真的很有趣。对我来说，使用AI本身就充满乐趣，因为A，它不是完全可预测的。（00:43:57）：所以我认为不确定会得到什么结果的这种元素很重要。这就像一盒巧克力。B，每当想到"哇，五年前我们根本没有这些东西"时，我总是感到惊叹。AI当时就像，嗯，我们能做预测分析。我们可以用AI运行一些非常高级的回归分析，但它与现在的形式完全不可同日而语。在我看来，尝试所有新推出的AI产品真的非常有趣。（00:44:33）：我认为这很重要，因为与SaaS领域其他领域相比，AI领域的发展速度要快得多。在SaaS成熟时代，研究竞争对手很重要。如果你要建立一家SaaS公司，不每年跟踪Salesforce、ServiceNow等公司的主要发布版本，那简直是疯了。（00:45:03）：这和那类似，但现在每周都有重大新发布和新产品，而不是每年才有。所以我认为你必须紧跟所有...所有动态，并结合我们前面提到的观点——很多东西都需要亲自体验，而不仅仅是阅读。你不能只是读TechCrunch上的报道或关于新功能的推文。你必须亲自尝试，才能真正理解它是什么。
