turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: One is really, really, really stressing this idea of go play with this stuff. And I mean, when I say play, I really mean play in the psychological sense of there's a difference when you go in and you're kind of just trying to check the box and get a job done. There's a difference when you come in with a curiosity and you're kind of exploring, right. And it's both more fun and energizing, but also, I think you learn more through that. And so I've really tried to stress the value of play with these AI products. (00:47:36): And I kind of try to lead by example, by literally going and sharing out links or screenshots of the things that I'm doing in these various products. So, as an example, I will go into one of the prototyping tools and show, "Hey, I built a marketing landing page for this new capability we're launching." I created a landing page for it in Replit, let's say, and now I'm sharing that link. Instead of what typically we would've done in the past is like, okay, we're going to write a doc about it and then share the doc, I'm just going to show you an actual landing page with visuals and everything in there. (00:48:20): Or I'll share the actual link to my deep research reports. Or instead of me writing a perfect memo on a topic, I'll actually just prompt my way into getting a chat thread or a chat output that basically covers all the content that I care about and maybe even ask it to, "Okay, summarize this all into a final memo output," and then intentionally share that rather than expose the fact that I'm using AI in this way and here's literally how I'm prompting it so you can follow along as well. (00:48:49): But really trying to encourage everyone to go and just play with these products. And I've even said, "Look, if anyone wants to just literally block out a day or frankly even a week and have the ultimate excuse, you could use... you could say that I told you to do it, right. If you want to cancel all your meetings for a day or for an entire week and just go play around with every product, AI product that you can find that you think could be relevant to Airtable, go do it. Period. So I think that's the most important thing is this play, this experimentation. (00:49:25): I think there's also a lot of other kind of shifts in how we execute prototypes over decks. I want to see actual interactive demos because, again, it's hard to... In a deck or in a PRD, you could say, "Okay. Well, we're going to make Omni really good at handling this kind of app building." Okay, those are just words. The real proof is in the pudding of like, "Okay, let me try it out on a few realistic prompts that I can imagine." (00:49:49): And in a demo, in a real prototype, you can instantly try it out on unrealistic rather than golden pathy scenarios and see how it feels too. Does it feel too slow? Do we need to expose more of the reasoning or steps that are happening behind the scenes? Create a progress bar or something like that. But it's really hard to get that feel of the product with anything but a functional prototype that really does, in an open-end way, use the AI to do whatever you put in. (00:50:24): So I think it's more like a experimentation playground it feels like how we need to execute, versus I think, in the past, it sometimes felt like a more deterministic resourcing and kind of timelines view of execution. We're going to put this many people on this problem, and this is the eight-week timeline to this milestone, and then we're going to ship in a quarter from now. And I think now the whole thing is just a lot more experimentation and iteration-driven.
turns.zh:
有一件事我一直在反复强调，那就是要真正去玩转这些人工智能产品。我说的“玩”，其实是从心理层面来讲的——当你只是为了完成任务而敷衍了事时，和带着好奇心去探索是完全不同的。这种探索不仅更有趣、更能激发创造力，还能让人学到更多东西。所以我一直致力于向大家传达玩转人工智能产品的价值。（00:47:36）  

我也会以身作则，直接分享我在这些产品中的操作成果。比如，我会进入某个原型设计工具，展示：“嘿，我为我们即将推出的新功能搭建了一个营销着陆页。”假设我在Replit上创建了这个页面，现在就把链接分享给大家。过去我们可能只是写一份文档说明，但现在我直接展示实际的着陆页，配上视觉效果和所有内容。（00:48:20）  

我还会分享深度研究报告的实际链接。与其写一份完美备忘录，我更愿意用自然语言生成工具生成聊天输出，再将其总结成最终的备忘录，这样既能传达关键信息，又不暴露我的操作过程，让大家能跟上节奏。（00:48:49）  

最重要的是，我鼓励大家去真正玩转这些产品。我甚至说过：“如果有人想专门腾出一天甚至一周时间，找个绝佳借口，那就用我给的理由。只要你想取消所有会议，花一天或一周时间探索所有与Airtable相关的AI产品，就去做吧。” （00:49:25）  

在原型设计和演示文稿方面也需要转变思路。我希望看到真实的交互式演示，因为文字描述总是有限的。比如，演示中可以说：“好，我们要让Omni在应用开发方面变得非常出色。” 但真正的证明在于实际体验——让用户尝试一些现实的场景，感受其真实表现。（00:49:49）  

在演示原型中，你可以即时测试非理想情境，观察用户反应。比如，速度是否过慢？是否需要展示更多幕后逻辑？添加进度条之类的元素。唯有能真正开放式使用AI功能的原型，才能最真实地传达产品体验。（00:50:24）  

所以我认为这更像是一个实验平台，而非过去那种按部就班的执行模式。过去我们会说：“我们要投入这么多人力资源，按八周时间表完成这个里程碑，然后在下个季度上线。”但现在整个过程更强调探索和实验。
迭代驱动的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of the different functions on a product team, PM, engineering design, who has had the most success being more productive with these tools, and how do you think this will impact each of these three functions over time?
turns.zh: 在产品团队的不同职能中，产品经理（PM）和工程设计人员中，哪一方的效率提升最显著？您认为随着时间推移，这三种职能将如何受到AI工具的影响？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: What I found is that it really does become more about individual attitude and maybe some polymathism. There's a strong advantage to any of those three roles who can kind of cross over into the other two, like the hybrid unicorn types. (00:51:26): So if you're a designer who can be just technical enough to kind of be dangerous and understand a little bit of how these models work and how does tool calling work and all of this stuff, then you can actually design a concept or even prototype a concept, including in these prototyping tools that's much more interesting and maybe realistic than if you're just stuck in the flat like let me put something in a static design concept because I think designs have to be more interactive. The whole... The value of the product and the [inaudible 00:52:04]-
turns.zh: 我的发现是，这实际上更多地取决于个人的态度和可能的多面手特质。三种角色中任何一种若能跨界到其他两个领域，比如混合型全能人才，都将具有明显优势。（00:51:26）：比如，如果你是一名设计师，具备足够的技术能力去理解模型运作原理、工具调用机制等，那么你就能设计出更具趣味性和可行性的概念或原型，而不仅仅局限于静态设计。这比被困在固有思维中（比如“让我把东西放进静态设计概念里”，因为他们认为设计必须更具互动性）要强得多。整个……产品的价值和[00:52:04不可听清]

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: ... the value of the product and the product functionality is in the interaction of it, right? Think about the design of Chachi Petite. Again, it's the most basic design you could possibly imagine. The real design actually is happening underneath the hood in how it responds to different queries and what happens after you fire off a prompt, right? So I think I found that there are people within each of these functions, there are engineers who are very good at thinking about product and experience and can go and prototype out the whole thing. They're designers who can do the same. Even if they can't literally code, they can prototype something out literally using a prototyping tool. (00:52:42): I think that's where AI tooling is also giving more advantage to people who can think in this way by equipping them with an alternative to actually having to go through the long hoops of learning CS, right? Then PMs as well. I think there are some PMs who are really getting into the technical details and studying up on how does this stuff work and actually getting hands-on, rather than seeing the role as writing documents, writing PRDs.
turns.zh: ……产品的价值和产品功能在于交互性，对吧？以Chachi Petite的设计为例。它看似是最基础的设计，但真正的设计在于底层逻辑——如何响应不同查询，以及在你触发提示后会发生什么。因此，我发现每个职能中都有这样的人：工程师能很好地思考产品和体验，并能用原型工具完整呈现设计；设计师也能做到这一点。即使他们不会写代码，也能用原型工具快速完成设计。（00:52:42）：我认为AI工具为具备这种思维方式的人提供了更多优势，让他们无需耗费大量精力学习计算机科学。项目经理也是如此。我注意到有些PM正在深入技术细节，研究这些工具如何运作，并亲自上手操作，而不再局限于写文档、PRD等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you see one of these roles, I don't know, being more in trouble than others, just like you need fewer of these people in the future potentially?
turns.zh: 您是否认为其中某个职位可能面临更大挑战，比如未来对这类人才的需求会减少？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I think overall you can get more done with fewer people, and that's not to say we want to go and make the team smaller, but rather ... the really cool thing for us and I think a lot of other companies is it's not like you have a finite set of things you need to do and execute on from a product standpoint, and okay, now I can do that with a 10th of people. I mean, you could do that in a lot of cases, but for us, maybe it's also because we're a very meta product, right? We are the app platform with which you can build now any AI app with AI, right? The apps themselves leverage AI capabilities at runtime, whether it's to generate imagery for a creative production workflow or leveraging deep research, or AI-based crawling of the web to search for companies that match a certain criteria for your Dealflow app or something like that. (00:54:10): We can effectively leverage all of these other AI capabilities in this app platform, because by definition we're enabling our customers to build apps that have this wide range of AI capabilities. But because of that, it's like we have a almost infinite set of possible AI capabilities that we could execute on, right? I'm always telling the team like, "Look, the great news is it's like we have all these fruit trees and there's so many crazy low-hanging fruit, and you've got literally massive watermelons literally sitting on the ground and all you have to do is walk over 20 feet and pick it up instead of having to climb the really tall coconut tree to grab a hard coconut from 50 feet up. So there's so many watermelons on the ground, just go out and start finding the biggest ones and attacking those, right?" (00:55:03): What that means is that if we can build this culture, and I do think it's a learnable way of operating, I really like to believe in the growth potential of any human and any individual. I think if you really have a growth mindset, and that's why one of our most important core values is growth mindset, right? If you really have that growth mindset, I think especially if you're willing to put in the nights and weekends hours, or in my case I'm literally telling people like, take a full day off, take a full week off and learn this stuff, you can become more fluent in this way. I think then what we get is a team that can just go and work on more things in a much more leveraged and fast way, right? (00:55:48): So, I like to think people who are willing to jump on the train are just going to become more and more effective. It's not like, oh, as a PM my role is becoming entirely irrelevant, right? No, it means that as a PM you need to start looking more like a hybrid PM prototyper who has some good design sensibilities. By the way, I think some of the best eng PM and design cultures respectively over the past even few decades have always been multidisciplinary in nature, right? The original PM spec at Google required the PMs to actually be somewhat technical so they could understand the engineering limitations of the product designs they wanted to make, and they had to be kind of designy, right? (00:56:33): I remember my co-founder, Andrew, when he was in the APM program was always reading books about design, even down to visual design and color theory and that kind of thing, right? So I think it's just a reminder that designers as well, some of the best designers through designer to Apple, including hardware designer, you have to understand some of the technical capabilities of how this stuff works, right? If you're an engineer, I think some of the best engineers and maybe Stripe always had a very good engineering culture of engineers who could think about the product and business requirements. In fact, on any given product group, at Stripe my understanding is that the DRI isn't always the PM as is traditionally the case in that triangle. Sometimes it's actually the engineer who's taking the product lead and saying, this is what we need to build.
turns.zh:
我认为总体而言，少人也能完成更多工作。这并不是说我们想缩小团队规模，而是……对我们和许多其他公司来说，真正酷的是——从产品角度来看，并非所有任务都需要固定的执行方案。比如，我们现在可以用十分之一的团队规模来实现同样的目标。当然，许多情况下确实可以做到，但对我们而言，可能还因为我们是一个元级产品，对吧？我们是应用平台，用户可以在此构建任何基于AI的应用。无论是为创意制作流程生成图像、利用深度研究，还是通过网络爬虫为Dealflow应用搜索符合特定标准的公司等，这些应用本身都会在运行时调用AI功能。由于我们的平台天生就支持客户构建具备广泛AI能力的应用，因此我们可以有效利用几乎无限的AI功能组合。正因如此，我们面临着几乎无穷无尽的AI可能性——就像有无数低垂的果实等着我们去摘取。（00:54:10）我总是对团队说：“好消息是，我们有满树的果实，地上有很多触手可及的西瓜。只需走过去就能摘到，而不是爬上50英尺高的椰子树去摘硬椰子。”地上的西瓜多得是，快去找最大的，然后全力攻克它们吧！（00:55:03）这意味着，如果我们能营造这种文化氛围——我相信这是一种可习得的运营方式——我深信每个人都具有成长潜力。只要你拥有成长型思维模式（这也是我们最重要的核心价值观之一），只要你愿意投入夜间和周末时间学习，你就能快速提升能力。我相信这样就能打造出一个能更高效、更快速开展工作的团队！（00:55:48）所以，我相信愿意跟上时代的人会变得越来越高效。这并不意味着产品经理的角色会被彻底边缘化——恰恰相反，产品经理需要转变为兼具设计能力的混合型角色。说真的，过去几十年来，最优秀的工程PM和设计文化往往是多学科融合的。谷歌最初的PM规范就要求PM具备一定的技术素养，以理解产品设计的工程限制，同时还要有设计敏感。（00:56:33）我记得我的联合创始人安德鲁在APM项目中就一直在研读设计书籍，甚至深入到视觉设计和色彩理论等领域。设计师也是如此，苹果的硬件设计师等顶级设计师都必须理解技术底层逻辑。工程师同样如此，Stripe等公司培养的顶级工程师往往具备设计思维。
工程师们拥有非常出色的工程文化，他们能够从产品和业务需求的角度进行思考。事实上，在Stripe的任何产品团队中，我了解到，产品负责人的角色（DRI）并不总是像传统三角结构中那样由产品经理担任。有时，真正承担产品主导职责的，其实是负责该产品的工程师，他们会主动提出：“这是我们需要开发的功能。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what I'm hearing is essentially the trend across product engineering design is each of those functions needs to get good at one of the other functions at least.
turns.zh: 这么说，我听到的基本趋势是，在产品工程设计领域，每个职能都需要至少精通其他某个职能。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ideally you can do them all, but if you can just do one additional, so a PM becomes better at design, an engineer becomes better at product management.
turns.zh: 理想情况下，你能全部掌握，但如果你能额外精通其中一项，比如产品经理在设计方面更出色，工程师在产品管理方面更擅长。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Well, I would actually go further and say I think you need to get decently good at all three. There's just a minimum baseline of if you're any one of those roles, you need to be minimally good at the other two, and then you can go deeper into your own specialty, right? You could be a designer who's really good at thinking about UX and interaction design, and then just good enough to be dangerous on thinking about what's technically possible and what is the product story around this feature.
turns.zh: 嗯，我甚至会更进一步说，我认为你需要在这三个方面都达到不错的水平。最低标准是，如果你担任其中任何一个角色，就需要在其他两个方面至少达到及格水平，然后你才能深入发展自己的专长，对吧？你可以是一位在用户体验和交互设计方面非常出色的设计师，同时在技术可行性以及该功能的产品定位方面也足够优秀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. To do that, one piece of advice that comes up again and again in what you've been describing is use the tools constantly to see what's possible, and that will teach you a lot of these things.
turns.zh: 我很赞同。要做到这一点，在你所描述的内容中反复出现的一个建议就是，不断使用相关工具去探索可能性，借此你能学到很多东西。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I think, well, use the tools gives you exposure to what's possible, right? It's kind of like if you wanted to be a great industrial designer, and let's say, I mean, the chair is the ultimate hello world of industrial design, it's the canonical design object, you wouldn't just sit there in a vacuum with no familiarity with the materials that you can use, plywood, steel, whatever, or existing form factors of chairs trying to invent the world's best chair in a vacuum, right? You should go and first do a study of all of the best chairs out there today. Go look at an Eames chair, sit in it and try to examine it to reverse engineer how it was made, and just look at the prior art for that type of product. That's how I see the go out and play with these products, and also, I think actually going and designing or implementing or executing is the best practice. (00:59:21): So you can't just only go and look at other people's chairs, eventually you have to go and actually try building your own and then try building another one and another one and another one. So, I think that's where ... when I think about how I hone my own product UX sensibilities, I never ... and at that time that I was in school and then learning about this stuff, there wasn't really any good curriculum for UX, right? It's not like there were great college classes to learn product UX. I mean, even CS was very academic in nature at that time, it wasn't applied software engineering, like build an app or whatever. Maybe now at some of the schools like Stanford, MIT, they have actually UXy type courses, but it's still a rarity for most people to have access to that. (01:00:03): So, the way I learned all of my product sensibilities was just trial and error and also using and studying other products, and then going and trying to build my own weekend project ideas, right? Oh, I want to build a Yelp style app with a map view and then also a list view, and I want it so that when you pan around in the map for it to automatically update the list view. Maybe there's some UX improvements I can make on top of that, but I can also test my technical skills to figure out which parts of this are hard to implement and how do you make it work, and what are some of the design changes or affordances that you can use to map to the technical possibilities.
turns.zh: 我觉得，嗯，使用这些工具能让你了解到什么是可能的，对吧？这就好比如果你想成为一名优秀的工业设计师。假设——我是说椅子是工业设计的入门级作品，是经典的设计对象——如果你不去了解可用的材料，比如胶合板、钢材之类的，或者现有的椅子设计形态，而是一味地闭门造车去发明“世界上最棒的椅子”，那是不可能的，对吧？你应该先去研究当下市面上所有优秀的椅子。去看看伊姆斯椅，坐进去仔细观察，逆向拆解它的制作工艺，研究同类产品的先例。对我来说，去实践这些产品才是最好的学习方式。我认为实际动手设计、实施和执行才是最佳实践。（00:59:21）：所以你不能只看别人的椅子，最终你必须亲手尝试制作一把，然后再做一把、再做一把……所以我觉得……当我思考如何磨练自己的产品用户体验敏感度时，我从不……当时我在学校学习这些知识时，并没有真正意义上的优秀用户体验课程，对吧？那时甚至连计算机科学课程也偏向学术性质，并非应用软件工程，比如开发应用程序之类的。或许现在像斯坦福、麻省理工这样的学校已经开设了用户体验类课程，但对大多数人来说，能接触到这类课程的机会仍然凤毛麟角。（01:00:03）：所以我学习所有产品设计敏锐度的方式就是不断尝试和错误，同时研究其他产品，然后去尝试制作自己的周末项目创意。比如，我想开发一个带有地图视图和列表视图的Yelp风格应用，还要实现当你在地图上滑动时，列表视图能自动更新。或许我能在此基础上进行一些用户体验优化，但我也能测试自己的技术能力，看看哪些部分难以实现，以及如何让它正常运行，还有哪些设计改进或交互方式能与技术可能性相契合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To do that, I loved your piece of advice, which I forgot to double down on, which I also find really powerful. The best tip there is find something to actually build that is useful to you and fun. Pick a project that's like, okay, this would be fun to do. Have a problem you're solving that forces you to actually do this thing.
turns.zh: 为了做到这一点，我很欣赏你的建议，但我之前没能加倍重视它，我也觉得这个建议非常有力。最重要的建议就是找一些对你有用又有趣的东西去实际制作。选择一个你觉得有趣的项目，解决一个迫使你必须动手去做的问题。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: For sure. Look, I think that can be night and weekend projects, it can also be the daytime job projects, right? I mean, I am basically telling our teams on the AI platform group especially, "Look, in that low hanging fruit metaphor, it's like I'm not being prescriptive with you on which watermelons you should pick, but you should go ..." We do have different pods within that group, but one of them for instance is what we call the field agents team and they're responsible for the agents that work within your app. So this is not the agent that builds your app, but these agents that run on a customer's behalf to do web research on your customers, or they can go and analyze a document and in the future maybe do things like actually generate a prototype of a feature from a PRD or from a feature idea. (01:01:52): I'm telling them, "Look, there's a almost infinite number of superpowers you can give these field agents. I'm not going to tell you which specifically to do. Now you can ask me to weigh in for sure, but you should go and just experiment and prototype a few different directions we could go." What if you prototype what it would look like to have a deep research implementation in field agents, so that for any given row of data, let's say in your case it's podcast guests, you can just click a button or click a button en masse across every speaker you have lined up to do deep research powered by ChatGPT's own deep research on each of the speakers and have them all laid out side by side in this table, right? Go prototype that and see how it feels and looks like. So I think some of this stuff can also be in your daytime job, especially if that daytime job is literally to go and build AI functionality.
turns.zh: 没错。听着，我觉得这些既可以是晚上或周末的项目，也可能是日常工作的任务，对吧？我的意思是，我基本上是在对我们AI平台团队说——“听着，用那个‘低垂的果实’比喻来说，我不是在规定你们该摘哪颗西瓜，而是让你们去……” 我们这个团队里有不同的组别，比如其中一个叫“现场代理团队”，负责处理应用内的代理服务。这些代理不是开发应用的团队，而是代表客户执行任务的——比如在网页上为用户做研究，或者分析文档。未来或许还能基于PRD或功能需求生成原型。（01:01:52）我对他们说：“听着，你们可以赋予这些现场代理几乎无限的‘超能力’。我不会具体告诉你们该怎么做。现在你可以来找我咨询，但你们应该去尝试，探索几个可能的方向。” 比如，你们可以设计一个在现场代理中进行深度研究的功能。针对任何一行数据，比如你们的播客嘉宾列表，只需点击一个按钮，或批量点击所有预约的嘉宾，就能通过ChatGPT对每位嘉宾进行深度研究，并将结果并排列在表格中。去实现这个功能看看效果如何。我觉得有些创意也可以融入日常工作，尤其是当日常工作本身就是开发AI功能的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually tried to do exactly that. The problem I ran into, I wonder if it's changed, is there's no API for ChatGPT deep research yet as far as I know.
turns.zh: 我其实尝试过这样做。但遇到的难题是，据我所知，ChatGPT的深度研究API目前还没有对外开放。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: There is now, there is now.
turns.zh: 现在已经开放了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There is, there we go.
turns.zh: 是的，可以用了。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Sometimes it ends up being ... and I think they only recently exposed it. It ends up being something on the order of a dollar plus per research call, which-
turns.zh: 有时候结果会……我觉得他们最近才开放这个功能。每次深度研究的费用大概一美元多——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a deal.
turns.zh: 太划算了。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: ... I mean, again, exactly. I mean, some people would say, oh my god, that's so expensive, and you rack up 50 of those, you've cost $50 a month. I think it's like, well, it just saved you hours of research by a human.
turns.zh: ……我的意思是，确实如此。有些人可能会说，天哪，这太贵了，一个月50次搜索就得50美元。但我觉得这比让人类花数小时研究要划算得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not only that, I actually have a researcher that I pay to give me background on guests that was four or 500 bucks and the dollar sounds great. I've been doing this-
turns.zh: 不仅如此，我之前雇了一个研究员帮我收集嘉宾背景资料，每次要花四五百美元，而一美元听起来很便宜。我一直在做这个——

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: [inaudible 01:03:28]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... I've been doing this manually.
turns.zh: ……我一直都是手动操作的。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: If he was being smart he would be using deep research and they just collected [inaudible 01:03:33]
turns.zh: 如果他聪明点，就会用深度研究功能，他们可能已经在用了。天啊，好吧，还有一个技能我想快速提一下。这些讨论中经常提到的是评估（evals）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They might be. They might just be. Oh, man. Okay, there's one more skill I wanted to talk about real quick. This comes up a lot in these conversations is evals.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The power of getting good at evals, I know that's something you value highly. Talk about just why you think this is something people need to get good at.
turns.zh: 掌握评估技巧的重要性，我知道这对您来说至关重要。请谈谈您为何认为人们有必要在评估方面下足功夫。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, and I listened to your episodes with [inaudible 01:03:54] and Mike who talked about this. I think it's interesting that both heads of OpenAI and Anthropic have converged on this point. I mean, look, I think I would add a slightly different or additive take though, which is I think for a completely novel product experience or form factor, you should actually not start with evals and you should start with vibes, right? Meaning you need to go and just test in a much more open-ended way, like, does this even work in kind of a broad sense? (01:04:28): So as an example, for our custom code generation capability, instead of defining evals that get repeatably tested as you vary the prompt or the model or the agentic workflow used to generate these outputs, and you have to define what does good look like by definition for the eval, I would first start with a much more open-ended and ad hoc style of just throw stuff against the wall, try different prompts and see how well it does. (01:05:01): To me, evals are more useful, A, once you've converged on the basic scaffold of the form factor and you kind of know what are the use cases you want it to work well for and what you want to test against it. Whereas in the early days, especially if your product market fit finding either for an entirely new company or for a pretty dramatically new or bold new capability that doesn't really have ... it's not an incremental improvement on something that exists in Airtable today, I think you have to just be a little bit more creative initially and throwing stuff at it, seeing what works to understand, okay, let's use an example, we're implementing this new capability that can use basically a long-running AI crawler agent that goes and researches the web for a specific type of object or entity, right? (01:05:55): So it's similar to deep research, but what it actually does is instead of outputting a report, it's actually going and compiling a list of things. The things could be companies or people or anything else, right? Find me every Marvel movie ever made, find me every DC Comics spin-off series, literally anything. You have to go in and first just try out a bunch of random ... use your own brain to think of what's the range of use cases I can test this against, right? Then you get back some results and you're like, okay, well, it's clear that where it does really well are these types of searches, people and companies with this kind of parameter. (01:06:42): I think to me, evals are useful once you have a sense of what is that cluster of useful use cases, you can start then more programmatically measuring the changes that you're making to improve the output for that, right? But by that point, you've probably already scoped the product and maybe the way we would merchandise it in Airtable is not a completely open-ended capability, but hey, here's a specific capability that can research one of these X number of entity types including people and companies, and here's even the filter conditions or criteria that are more explicit that you can define to give it the prompting to search for that thing, right? (01:07:25): But I kind of think it's more useful as a way to iterate your way to improvement, and you can start really testing stuff empirically, right? You can A/B test, especially if you have the scale of a really large product like Anthropic or OpenAI, you can just test everything and see like, oh, this model actually performs better than this one, this prompt performs better than this one, but I think early on you don't have that luxury and you're in a much more open-ended discovery process.

turns.zh: 我认为，要真正、真正努力打破角色壁垒，这一点对EPND来说无疑是正确的，在典型的EPD三角关系中亦是如此。但我认为，即使对非产品类角色来说，这一点也很有道理，对吧？比如在市场营销领域也是如此，对吧？这是我在市场营销部门大力推动的，而且我认为我们的营销团队也确实在积极践行——如果你能亲自完成所有工作……传统上，营销团队的运作方式可能是这样：有一个人负责执行营销活动中的效果营销部分。他们直接进入Google AdWords界面，调整定向、预算和转化跟踪等参数；而另一个人则专门负责撰写广告文案；还有人负责制定种子内容或定位指南（由产品营销经理提供），以支持广告创意的制作，等等。或许他们还需要推广某个新制作的演示素材。（01:10:35）：我认为，就像你能在EPD中打破角色壁垒一样，最理想的人选或许在某个维度上深耕专精，比如工程领域，但又要足够全面，以至于在其他两个维度上也能游刃有余。我认为这种理念几乎适用于所有其他职能部门，对吧？比如销售部门，你也应该开始更多地承担SE的角色。传统上，销售人员对产品了解不深，需要SE来介入充当产品专家。如今要销售任何AI产品，如果不精通产品并能进行产品演示，那简直难上加难，因此AE也需要精通SE的知识。（01:11:21）：所以我认为，打破角色壁垒的理念是，每个人都需要变得更加全能，以结果为导向，对吧？作为AE，你的目标是让客户相信产品的价值并达成交易，对吧？好吧，要做到这一点，你过去需要依赖营销部门创建的资产和SE的演示支持。能否减少这些依赖，让你完全可以独立完成所有工作呢？我认为这对每一家AI原生公司或希望在新领域竞争的公司来说，都是一种全新的运营思维。

(01:14:38): What that means in an organizational context is you then create these different fiefdoms, you hire all these execs and each exec just manages their own swim lane, and there's relatively looser coupling between all of those different groups, right? (01:15:05): Using the factory metaphor of there's an argument that that's actually kind of an efficient way to scale up production for each of these different swim lanes, right? 我听过你对布莱恩·切斯基的采访，之后你在YC静修会上谈到创始人模式，这些观点真的让我深有共鸣。我觉得，或许用不那么华丽的语言，我也从自身经历中领悟到了一些相同的原则。当你扩张规模时——这也与我们之前讨论的公司早期阶段相关——你需要深陷细节之中，寻找产品与市场的契合点，你必须具备多面手的能力，对吧？从技术层面到设计，再到商业模式，甚至免费增值模式的设定，以及如何推广产品，网站设计等，这些决策都息息相关，对吧？你无法将它们割裂开来，然后各自独立生产。它们相互交织，你需要一个紧密合作的小团队，全面统筹所有这些工作。（01:14:04）：在我看来，只有这样才能首先创造出神奇的产品与市场契合点。然后当你扩张规模时，运营专家和大型公司投资者常给出的建议是，嗯，你得把所有这些流程标准化，对吧？这就像从手工制作单件服装的工匠，转向工厂化生产，对吧？（01:14:38）：在组织层面，这意味着你会创建不同的部门，聘请各路高管，每个高管只管自己的一亩三分地，不同部门间联系松散。对吧？所以销售部门只管销售，市场部门只管市场，产品部门只管产品。甚至在产品部门内部，不同的产品组和模块也各自为战。（01:15:05）：用工厂比喻来说，有人认为这确实是扩展生产的有效方式，对吧？每个部门都能更自主地专注于规模化增长，等待，如何生产更多产品？如果某个产品组致力于改进搜索功能，那就是我们的核心任务。我们就只管不断迭代，改进搜索功能。所以人们给出这种建议并不全无道理，但我认为这样做会失去整体思维的神奇整合价值，失去对大局的战略把握。（01:15:48）：我觉得布莱恩在与你的那期节目中多次强调这一点，他说，在真正重视产品的公司里，首先，我很赞同他提到的CEO必须扮演首席产品官的角色，你必须关心产品。最终产品才是核心，你不能永远依赖于扩展市场来维持产品竞争力，你必须持续创新产品。顺便说一句，创新产品的最佳方式不是在各个细分领域进行渐进式改进，而是要有更宏大的、阶跃式的愿景，思考产品如何实现飞跃，或者产品下一个重大功能、能力或重塑。（01:16:35）：所以我认为，如果你真的想从产品执行的角度定期重新发现新的产品与市场契合点，就必须在整个公司推行完全不同的运营和领导模式。
组织层面。关于如何在人工智能原生时代运营的所有讨论，我认为其核心要点与在产品市场不断寻求适配状态时所需的运营方式完全一致。（01:17:02）：我完全赞同这样一个理念——你必须以宏观视野思考，推动整个组织朝着更宏大的目标迈进，同时在这个时代里要更加频繁地交付成果、学习总结和进行实验。那么，从上述内容中我得到的启发是，具体建议固然有其合理性，比如按某种方式扩大规模、招聘具备经验的运营人员等等——这些建议显然有其道理，毕竟提出建议的人并非无能之辈，他们的建议在特定情境下确有其效。但我认为更深层的启示在于，不能简单地照搬他人的建议。比如，许多人给出的行动方案未必适合你所有人，因为每个人都有不同的先验假设，几乎就像我们都是各自的“语言模型”，其训练数据集源自我们独特的经验背景。或许你接受的训练是基于某项服务——

turns.en: ... experiences, and maybe you're trained on like the kind of ServiceNow or the Oracle training corpus, and this person's trained on the Facebook corpus, and I'm trained on the Airtable one. (01:18:44): The answer might be like, "Hey, at So-and-So company, this is how we eliminated the PM role entirely." For Brian at Airbnb, it made sense. We're no longer having PMs in their traditional form. Now, we have program managers and product marketers, but more than the actual decision because I don't think it's a one-size-fits-all, everybody should do the same, why did you do that? The why actually was very informative, and then be able to take that and say like, "Okay, how would I apply that?" Maybe it yields a different outcome, but the reasoning actually is very informative.
turns.zh: ……这些经验，或许你接受过ServiceNow或Oracle的培训课程，而这个人接受过Facebook的培训课程，而我则接受过Airtable的培训课程。我认为我越来越努力做的，不是忽视聪明人的建议——显然那不是正确的做法，而是认真倾听他们的意见。这就像在LLM中，现在你可以借助推理模型来审视整个思维链条，了解它是如何得出这个答案的。对我来说，“你为什么推荐这个？”这样的提问比“就按这个建议做吧”更有价值。（01:18:44）答案可能是：“嘿，在某某公司，我们就是这样彻底取消了项目经理角色的。” 这对Airbnb的布莱恩来说很有意义。我们不再沿用传统的项目经理模式，现在有项目经理和产品营销人员，但重点不在于具体的决策方式——我不认为存在一刀切的方案，每个人都应该照做。更重要的是要理解背后的逻辑。为什么会这样做？这种逻辑分析能提供更深刻的见解，然后你可以借鉴这些思路，说：“好吧，我该如何应用这些经验？” 或许会产生不同的结果，但这种推理过程本身就极具价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how this idea founder mode is not so different from this ICCO trend that you're following and it's-
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这种创始人模式和你们正在追随的ICCO趋势并没有太大差别——

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: For sure.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... yeah, yeah, it's like being in the weeds, being in the details, trying things yourself, not delegating to execs.
turns.zh: ……是啊，是啊，这就像深陷细节，亲自尝试各种方法，而不是把事情交给高管们处理。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, and I think anything taken to an extreme can be problematic. There is a world where you are so in the details and in every detail that you're basically just micromanaging and you're kind of creating like a euphemism for that. That's not really what founder mode is about. That's not like the Brian conception of founder mode is to like micromanage everything and not trust anyone, but I think it's more about finding that right balance of being unabashed about caring about the details that do matter and where the tying together of details across different groups or departments actually is the only way to yield a non-incremental outcome. Otherwise, each person is just optimizing within their own domain, but you'll never get to the global maxima or the global breakthrough. (01:20:23): I think the really cool thing about CEOs as I seize it, frankly any leader playing more of an IC-like role and being in the details is I think for the right type of person, it's actually more fun that way. I mean, to be honest, for me, the times where I felt most disintermediated from what I felt was the substance of this company was when I thought that I was almost like forcing myself to step away from the details. I thought that's what a at-scale CEO was supposed to do. I mean, there's some famous CEOs who have talked about, "The less decision I could make the better. The less details I'm exposed to the better. I just want to inspect at the topmost layer how this business is running, and if everything underneath it is going smoothly, then I'm able to do that and everything looks good." (01:21:19): I just think that's maybe, again, it works in a certain type of very mature type of business. Even then, though, I can't imagine that at a CPG company like a Procter & Gamble. You wouldn't want to have a CEO who still actually goes and tastes the soup and tries the products and sees literally the details of what the new product innovation pipeline looks like, as well as like how it's being experienced on the shelves and so on. I don't know. I guess I'm just more and more skeptical that that hands-off pure delegation and process management role ever works as a CEO. Maybe you go through a long enough period of where the business is coasting that nobody notices, but I got to say, for me it's just much more invigorating to get to play that role. I think for the types of operators and leaders that I most admire, that's what makes the job interesting. They don't want to have a automated away kind of role as a leader.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得任何事情都可能走向极端都会带来问题。有些时候，你会深陷于细节之中，甚至过度微观管理，这其实是一种委婉的说法。这根本不是创始人模式的真谛。布莱恩对创始人模式的理解并非事事亲力亲为、不信任他人，而是要找到一个恰当的平衡——既要坦然关注重要细节，又要善于整合不同团队或部门的信息，最终才能实现非递增式的突破。否则，每个人都只在自己的领域内优化，但永远无法触及整体最优解或突破性成果。（01:20:23）：说实话，我认为CEO（或者任何扮演类似IC角色的领导者）深入细节的做法，如果是适合的人选，实际上会更有乐趣。对我来说，当我觉得自己与公司的核心业务脱节时，往往是因为强迫自己远离细节。我认为这才是大规模CEO该做的。有些知名CEO曾说：“我越少做决策越好。我越少接触细节越好。我只想在最高层面审视业务运作，只要底层一切顺利，我就能做到这一点，一切看起来都很美好。”（01:21:19）：但我认为这种模式可能只适用于某些成熟的业务。即便如此，我也无法想象在宝洁这样的快消公司中，CEO会亲自品尝汤品、试用产品、逐一审查新品创新流程的每个细节，以及观察产品在货架上的实际表现。我不知道，我越来越怀疑那种完全放手、只负责授权和流程管理的CEO模式是否可行。或许在业务平稳期，你可以暂时不被察觉，但说实话，我更享受亲力亲为的角色。我认为我最欣赏的那些运营者和领导者正是这种角色让工作充满趣味。他们不希望领导角色被自动化替代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you could go back in time and whisper something in a decade-ago Howie's ear that would have saved you a lot of pain and suffering over the last decade, what would that be?
turns.zh: 如果你能回到十年前，对豪伊耳语一句忠告，能为你省去过去十年的诸多痛苦与煎熬，那会是什么？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Don't step away from the details that both you love. I mean, first of all, if your passion is building product and product design, even if it feels like at times the company needs to do all this other stuff like scale up, go to market, and operations and just have like a large people organization, that itself creates a lot of need to do things and manage. There becomes a new job invented just to manage a larger group of people, and obviously you're going to have to do some of that. You can't just completely eschew all your responsibility as an at-scale CEO, but don't lose the essence of the thing that you love doing and that really made this product happen and gives this company as many companies that were founded on a magical product market fit finding insight. Don't step too far away from that, and always make sure that is still your number one, even if other stuff has to also add to your plate.
turns.zh: 不要偏离那些你深爱的细节。我想说，首先，如果你的热情在于产品开发和设计，即便有时公司需要处理扩张、市场推广、运营等事务，甚至组建庞大的团队，这些本身就需要大量管理工作。随之而来的是专门管理大型团队的新职位，而你显然必须承担其中一部分职责。你无法完全逃避作为大规模CEO的所有责任，但也不能失去自己热爱的事情——正是这些事物让产品得以问世，让这家公司得以成立，让无数基于神奇的产品市场契合点而创立的公司受益。不要偏离这些核心，始终将它们置于首位，即便其他事务也需要分担你的精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think people don't talk enough about this how if someone starts a company that's an idea they have they're excited about, it takes off and then you're stuck on that for a long time, and then even if things are pushed in a direction you're not as excited about. This point about just remembering what you actually love about it and coming back to that is so important because that's the only way to keep doing this for a long time.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们对此谈论得不够。比如，当有人创办一家公司时，他们对这个想法充满热情，产品一炮而红后，你就被困在其中很久，即便事态朝着你不那么兴奋的方向发展。这时候，记住自己真正热爱的东西并回归初心至关重要，因为这是长期坚持下去的唯一途径。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I think that's so true, and to me that's why there's always been a difference between entrepreneurs who love the act of building a product or the business, too, versus those who saw a just purely business or financial opportunity that they felt like they couldn't pass up exploiting or going after. Look, no knock on people who are more the latter, and there's entire industries where it's all just about alpha generation. You can go into the private equity business and so on, and it's just purely it's rationally about how do I find the alpha? I think that some of the best companies, product central companies, at least in my opinion, are run by those people who actually just love the product. I think you get a feel for that from some of the AI companies like Sam, I think genuinely just loves working on AI. (01:25:03): If he could spend a hundred percent of his time on just being close to the AI and the research, I mean, he would and he's even said as much. Ranging to like Brian's with Airbnb, it's pretty clear that people like this are not motivated like... Airbnb was not founded because like, "Oh my God, we want to make a lot of money off this arbitrage opportunity against hotels."
turns.zh: 我认为这点很对。在我看来，创业者要么热爱产品开发或商业运作，要么只是看到了纯粹的商业或财务机会，觉得不容错过。比如私募股权行业，核心就是如何捕捉超额收益。有些最出色的公司，尤其是以产品为核心的公司，至少在我看来，都是由真正热爱产品的人运营的。从Sam这样的AI公司就能感受到这一点——他显然热爱AI研究。（01:25:03）：如果他能把所有时间都投入到AI和研究中，我相信他会这样做，他也曾公开表示过。再看Brian创办的Airbnb，很明显，他们的动机并非“天哪，我们要利用酒店套利机会赚大钱”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They just needed to pay their rent.
turns.zh: 他们只是需要支付房租。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. Well, that and I think they loved the product and I think they also loved the way in which they built the product, the design-centric nature of that product and company and culture. That's what gives you the continued joy of working on what could be the same company for a very long time.
turns.zh: 是的。除此之外，我认为他们热爱产品，也热爱产品开发的方式，热爱产品的设计导向以及公司文化。正是这些，让你在同一家公司长期工作时始终充满乐趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Howie, is there anything else that you wanted to touch on or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 霍伊，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I just want to reiterate, especially for listeners here who are in an EP or D role and especially in the P role, I really do believe that this is not like you either have or you don't like in terms of the skill set needed to be relevant and AI needed, but I do think it's a call to action to go and bolster your skill sets where they may be less refined right now. I think even programming, I really believe everyone could learn how to be a software engineer if they wanted to. Now, obviously, some people just as with like great writers are never going to be a published author or the Hemingway, but everyone can gain a good enough proficiency of software engineering if they really wanted to. (01:26:39): You could take that boot camp. You could do like some coding exercises on the side, et cetera. The point there is that sometimes I think we treat these disciplines like hard, hard skills that if you're already halfway into your career and you're not already an engineer, if you're not already a designer, okay, well, you can never be one. I just think our brains are malleable and there's a lot of great curriculum out there to learn. Lot of it, like I said, just comes down to also like trial and error and building projects, maybe nights and weekends projects even to learn this stuff. Everyone can learn how to be a versatile kind of unicorn product engineer/designer hybrid in the AI-native era. The only thing stopping you is just going out and doing it.
turns.zh: 我只想再次强调，特别是对于在场的担任EP或D角色的听众，尤其是P角色的听众，我真的认为，在具备相关性和人工智能所需的技能方面，并非非此即彼的二元选择。但我认为这更像是一次行动号召，鼓励大家去提升那些目前尚不精通的技能。就连编程方面，我坚信只要有意愿，每个人都能学会如何成为一名软件工程师。当然，有些人就像伟大作家永远无法成为出版作家、海明威那样，但只要足够用心，每个人都能掌握足够扎实的软件工程技能。（01:26:39）你可以参加编程训练营，利用业余时间进行编码练习等等。关键在于，有时我们把这些技能视为高深莫测的硬技能，认为如果你已经步入职场中期，却非工程师或设计师，那就注定无缘了。我认为人的大脑是具有可塑性的，市面上有很多优质的学习资源。正如我所说，关键在于不断尝试和犯错，利用业余时间甚至周末项目来掌握这些技能。在人工智能时代，每个人都能成为全能型的“独角兽”产品工程师/设计师。唯一阻碍你的，就是迈出行动的那一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really empowering way to end it, and just to double down on that, it's never been easier to learn these things. There are super intelligences that you can talk to that do a lot as they're building can help you learn.
turns.zh: 这真是充满力量的收尾。再强调一遍，学习这些技能从未像现在这样简单。现在有超级智能助手能帮你学习，效果显著。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, literally, I go into ChatGPT sometimes and I ask it just like, "Hey, how would you build this app?" I'm just curious. I'm like, "How would you build Manus, the open-ended agent?" Literally, how would you build it? You can ask the questions and it's like having an amazing, brilliant software architect, software engineer, product manager, designer expert tutor that you can literally like there's no dumb question. They have infinite patience. They're literally on and awake 24/7. It is the most incredible time to learn this stuff, to your point. Then, of course, the interactive tools to go and actually build stuff. Anyone can download Cursor and just start asking Composer to generate some code for you, and then looking at the code and trying to figure out what it does. To your point, when I think back to the earliest era that I experienced of building apps, first I learned C++, then I learned PHP and JavaScript and even building kind of JavaScript single-page apps in the early days like '08 through 2010. It was a dark, dark art. I mean, there were some like... You just had to go and like learn some of these things. There wasn't great tutorials for it. You had to reverse engineer certain things. There were just weird things like if you wanted rounded corners in your UI, you literally took Photoshop, opened it up, created like a rounded corner in pixels, and then cut that pixel up into an image that you dropped onto the page at exactly the right position to be at the edge of a box. (01:29:15): It's like crazy stuff. I mean, everything was so much more arcane at the time, and now it feels so much more fluid and accessible, and the gap between the arcane tech that you have to wade through to build something has just been minimized so much. It's like the effort and abstraction between you and the magical, delightful actual building of the thing that you want has been so minimized. It's never been a more exciting time to be a builder.
turns.zh:
是啊。我是说，就字面意义上来说，我有时会进入ChatGPT，问它：“嘿，你怎么开发这个应用？”我只是好奇。我会问：“你怎么开发Manus这个开放式智能助手？”真的想知道你怎么开发它。你可以提问，感觉就像有位超棒、超聪明的软件架构师、工程师、产品经理、设计师专家导师在你身边——完全没有愚蠢的问题。他们耐心无限，日夜在线。正如你所说，现在是学习这些技术的最佳时机。

当然，还有互动工具能真正帮助你开发应用。任何人都可以下载Cursor，直接让Composer为你生成代码，然后查看代码并试图理解其功能。说到这儿，我回想起自己最早开发应用的时期——首先学习C++，然后是PHP和JavaScript，甚至在2010年前后开发过单页JavaScript应用。那真是个黑暗的时代。当时几乎全凭自己摸索，没有优质教程，必须逆向工程某些功能。比如，要在UI中实现圆角效果，你得用Photoshop创建像素圆角，再把像素裁剪成图片，准确放置在边框位置。（01:29:15）简直疯狂。当时一切都晦涩难懂，现在却流畅易用得多。从技术门槛到实际开发的跨度已经极大缩小。现在要成为开发者，真是最激动人心的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You remember spacer.gif?
turns.zh: 你记得spacer.gif吗？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Oh yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like to create. It's that line stuff you just kind of have-
turns.zh: 就像创建东西。就是那种你只需要——

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah, I remember it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，我记得。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... the invisible one-pixel thing that you just stick in places.
turns.zh: ……那个看不见的一像素的东西，你随便插在某个地方。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. No.
turns.zh: 是啊。是啊，不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, what a time to be alive. Howie, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 天哪，活在当下真是太棒了。霍伊，接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here we go. What are two or three books you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 开始吧。你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: You know, I've been trying to read fiction more, partly because I think it's just a really nice mental reset. I will say like Three-Body Problem for anyone who hasn't read it, it's a mind-expanding book. I like sci-fi and fiction that kind of opens your brain, so maybe this is my cheat card, but it's a three-book series. Those are three great books.
turns.zh: 你知道吗，我最近一直在努力多读些小说，部分原因是我觉得这能让大脑得到很好的放松。我要向没读过《三体》的人推荐它，这是一本能拓展思维的书。我喜欢能激发想象力的科幻和小说，也许这算我的推荐秘籍，但这是一个三部曲系列。这三本书都很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that series, and my tip there is it gets good one and a half books in is my tip, so just keep reading. That's where it's like, "Okay, now I'm in."
turns.zh: 我超爱这个系列，我的建议是读到一半左右就进入状态了。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: I liked even the first one, but I felt like it was inception where every subsequent book was like you dropped into another, like you incepted into another layer, right?
turns.zh: 甚至第一部我也很喜欢，但我觉得那部电影就像《盗梦空间》（Inception）一样，每本后续的书都像是你掉入了另一个层级，陷入了另一个梦境，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. What's a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: TV show, I just started watching The Studio. It's like the Seth Rogen, Rogen.
turns.zh: 电视剧的话，我刚开始看《The Studio》。它有点像塞斯·罗根（Seth Rogen）的风格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's so stressful.
turns.zh: 是啊，这部剧太紧张刺激了。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Yep. Yeah, it is pretty stressful, and I mean, Silicon Valley was too close to home when it came out, so I watched it, but it was just cringy. The Studio is kind of fund to watch because it's a little bit about like inside baseball of Hollywood, and yet I'm not in Hollywood, so it's entertaining to watch. It's I thought smart and a funny show because I split time between L.A. and S.F. I also feel like it's very real to me. I see a lot of the literal characters out there in the world that it's characterizing.
turns.zh: 没错。确实压力很大。我觉得《硅谷》（Silicon Valley）播出时太贴近现实生活了，所以我看了，但感觉有点尴尬。《The Studio》倒是挺有趣的，因为它讲的是好莱坞内部的运作机制，而我又不在好莱坞，所以看起来挺有意思的。我觉得这部剧既聪明又有趣，因为我常往返洛杉矶和旧金山。我觉得里面很多角色都和我在现实中见过一模一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really love? Could be an app, could be gadget, could be clothing.
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？可以是应用、电子产品、服装等等。

turns.speaker: Howie Liu
turns.en: Okay, so I'll give two because I feel like I have to say some kind of software product. I mean, I'm a really big fan of Runway, the product and the company. I just think every new model they come out with, they just came out with a new one just I think like two days ago that gives even more controls and refinement on creating exactly the video scene that you want. I think just the photorealism in what you can generate now, and they also built this cool demo thing that's an immersive world generator I mentioned before. I think it's just cool to see. I also like the underdog story. I'm clearly like Google's gunning in the space, has VO3 and so on and has its OpenAI, but I love the underdog story of this sub-hundred-person company still punching above their weight and building really awesome video experiences. That's the software one. Look, everybody has different circumstances. (01:37:06): I think I fully own that even though I didn't come from money, my family was very, very financially modest growing up. I still had incredible resources and opportunities afforded to me even just by virtue of growing up in the U.S., being born in and growing up in the U.S., but also having access to a computer and the internet and even all the free resources I could then access and learn about from there. I still feel like whatever you have or don't have to start with, if you kind of approach the world and kind of the future with a spirit of humility and gratitude rather than, I guess, the opposite of that, I think I've felt like it kind of becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. You're open-minded, you're kind of grateful, and then more opportunities actually come your way, and maybe it's because the energy you're putting out into the world and other people. (01:38:07): You're kind of attracting good opportunities and good people and good things, but I think there's a lot of other parts of his framework, but the one that is easiest to remember is like, how do I approach each day? 我偶然发现了保罗·康蒂（Paul Conti）这个人。据我所知，他既是一名医学博士，也是一名心理学家。他写过一本书，还和安德鲁·休伯曼（Andrew Huberman）做过一期长篇播客。播客中他主要探讨如何看待人生观，以及如何建立思考人生的框架，但这些观点都基于科学、神经学和认知科学的理论基础。其中有一点让我印象深刻，深有共鸣——那就是若能以谦逊和感恩为核心来构建生活方式。

（01:38:07）：你保持开放心态、心怀感恩时，机遇自然降临。这源于你向世界传递的正能量。他的理论框架中还有许多深刻见解，但最容易铭记的或许是：如何开启每一天？即便遭遇挫折——比如解雇员工、客户流失、设备故障等——仍能以谦逊感恩之心审视全局，这会改变你的心态，让积极能量渗透到当天乃至整个人生。
